articles.title: Aircraft Insurance Claims: What to Do After an Accident, NTSB 830 Reporting and How Hull Claims Are Settled
articles.description: After an aircraft accident: NTSB Part 830 notification, wreckage preservation, 10-day reports, and how aviation hull and liability claims settle.
articles.author: Insurance Bhaiya Research Desk
keyTakeaways: Under **49 CFR Part 830**, any accident (death, serious injury or *substantial damage*) and certain incidents require **immediate notification** to the NTSB.
Preserve the wreckage and records. You may move them only to help injured people, prevent further damage or protect public safety, and you must photograph and sketch first.
A written report on **NTSB Form 6120.1** is due **within 10 days** of an accident, or within 7 days if an aircraft is still missing.
Notify your insurer immediately too. Late notice and pilot-warranty breaches are the two most common reasons aviation claims run into trouble.

faqs.question: Do I have to report an aircraft accident to the NTSB?
faqs.answer: Yes. Accidents involving death, serious injury or substantial damage, and certain listed incidents, require immediate notification under 49 CFR 830.5, followed by Form 6120.1 within 10 days. See the [aircraft & aviation insurance explained](/learn/aircraft-aviation-insurance-explained/) hub.

faqs.question: Can I move the wreckage before the insurer sees it?
faqs.answer: Only to help injured people, prevent further damage or protect public safety, and you must photograph and sketch the scene first. Tell your insurer before you arrange salvage.

faqs.question: Will an aircraft insurance claim raise my premium?
faqs.answer: Usually yes at renewal, especially for in-motion hull claims caused by pilot error.

content.text: An [aviation insurance](/qa/aviation-products-liability-insurance/) claim runs alongside a federal reporting process, and getting the order right protects both your legal position and your claim. This spoke of our [aircraft & aviation insurance explained](/learn/aircraft-aviation-insurance-explained/) hub walks through the first hour, the first 10 days and the settlement.
Step 1: Is It an 'Accident' Under NTSB Part 830?

An aircraft accident is an occurrence associated with flight operations in which someone suffers death or serious injury, or the aircraft receives **substantial damage**. Substantial damage means damage needing major repair or replacement of a component. It excludes items such as dented skin, small punctures, bent fairings or, in many cases, landing gear damage alone. Certain incidents also require immediate notification even without an accident. Examples include flight control malfunctions, in-flight fires, crew incapacitation, propeller blade release, loss of 50% or more of cockpit displays, and damage to property other than the aircraft exceeding $25,000.
Step 2: The First Hour Checklist

items: Take care of injured people and call emergency services.
Notify the NTSB immediately if Part 830 applies.
Preserve the wreckage. Move it only to help injured people, prevent further damage or protect public safety, and photograph and sketch the original positions first.
Secure the logbooks, maintenance records and any flight data.
Call your insurer's claims line, or your broker, before you arrange salvage or repairs. For seaplanes, wreck removal has its own limit (see [seaplane insurance](/learn/seaplane-insurance/)).

content.title: Be Careful With Recorded Statements
content.text: Insurers, and other parties' insurers, may ask for a recorded statement early. You can usually ask to give it later or with counsel. See [can I refuse a recorded statement to an insurance company](/qa/can-i-refuse-a-recorded-statement-to-insurance-company/). Stick to facts in the NTSB report and avoid speculating about cause.
Step 3: How Hull Claims Are Settled

Most hull policies are written at an **agreed value**. If the aircraft is repairable, the insurer pays repair costs minus the [deductible](/glossary/deductible/), often with separate in-motion and not-in-motion deductibles. If repairs exceed a threshold, the aircraft is declared a total loss and the agreed value is paid, with the insurer usually taking the salvage. What is and isn't included (engine wear, pre-existing corrosion, loss of use) is covered in [what does aircraft hull insurance cover](/qa/what-does-aircraft-hull-insurance-cover/). If the aircraft was financed, the lender is paid first under the lienholder endorsement.
Step 4: Liability Claims and Subrogation

Injured passengers or property owners claim against your liability cover, which pays up to the policy limits and any per-seat sublimit (see [smooth vs per-seat](/compare/smooth-liability-vs-per-seat-sublimit-aircraft-insurance/)). If you were renting, the owner's insurer may pay the owner and then seek recovery from you through [subrogation](/glossary/subrogation/), which is where [private pilot insurance](/qa/private-pilot-insurance/) earns its premium. Instructors face the same exposure. See [flight instructor insurance](/qa/flight-instructor-insurance/). Hangar damage follows the split explained in [aircraft hangar insurance](/learn/aircraft-hangar-insurance/).

content.title: Most Common Reasons Aviation Claims Are Denied
content.text: The pilot didn't meet the pilot warranty. The annual inspection was expired. The flight was for hire under a pleasure-use policy. Notice to the insurer was late. If a claim is denied or closed unfairly, read [can an insurance company close a claim without my consent](/qa/can-an-insurance-company-close-a-claim-without-my-consent/) and [can you sue your insurance company](/qa/can-you-sue-your-insurance-company/). For the general claims process, see [what is an insurance claim](/learn/what-is-an-insurance-claim/).

After a claim, expect your renewal premium to rise. Your next quote will reflect the loss, which is one more reason to build experience as described in [airplane insurance cost](/learn/airplane-insurance-cost/). If an accident leaves you unable to hold a medical certificate, [pilot loss of license insurance](/qa/pilot-loss-of-license-insurance/) and [life insurance for pilots](/qa/does-life-insurance-cover-private-pilots/) are the income and family protection layers.

articles.title: Aircraft Hangar Insurance: Building Cover, Hangarkeepers Liability and What Your Hangar Lease Demands
articles.description: Aircraft hangar insurance explained: why your aircraft policy doesn't cover the building, hangarkeepers liability, and airport hangar lease requirements.
articles.author: Insurance Bhaiya Research Desk
keyTakeaways: Your aircraft hull policy protects the **airplane** inside the hangar, not the **hangar building**. The building needs its own property cover.
Tools, equipment and spare parts in the hangar may not be covered by your aircraft policy unless they're insured separately.
**Hangarkeepers liability** is for anyone who stores, maintains or services *other people's* aircraft: it covers aircraft in your care, custody or control.
Airport hangar leases commonly require liability minimums, proof of hull cover, and an additional-insured endorsement naming the airport authority.

faqs.question: Does my aircraft insurance cover my hangar?
faqs.answer: No. Hull cover protects the aircraft inside it. The building needs separate property insurance. See the [aircraft & aviation insurance explained](/learn/aircraft-aviation-insurance-explained/) hub.

faqs.question: What is hangarkeepers insurance?
faqs.answer: Liability cover for damage to other people's aircraft while they're in your care, custody or control, for example during storage, maintenance or servicing.

faqs.question: Does hangaring my plane lower my insurance premium?
faqs.answer: Usually, yes. Insurers favor hangared aircraft over tie-downs, especially in hail- and wind-exposed regions.

companionTool.description: Calculate your total protection requirement across life, health, and personal liability.

content.text: Hangaring an airplane usually lowers its insurance premium compared with an outdoor tie-down, especially in hail country, as [Brian's first Cessna 182 scenario](/scenarios/brian-first-cessna-182-texas/) shows. But owning or leasing a hangar creates exposures your aircraft policy doesn't cover. This spoke of our [aircraft & aviation insurance explained](/learn/aircraft-aviation-insurance-explained/) hub sorts out which policy covers what.
Four Hangar Exposures, Four Different Coverages

rows: Your aircraft damaged by hangar fire or roof collapse
The hangar structure, doors and electrical systems
Tools, tugs, spare parts and avionics on shelves
Contents cover or an equipment floater
A visitor trips over a tow bar
Damage to someone else's aircraft you store or work on

content.text: When You Need Hangarkeepers Liability

Hangarkeepers liability applies when you store aircraft belonging to others, perform maintenance on third-party aircraft, or run an aviation service business. Examples include renting a corner of your hangar to another owner, running an A&P shop, or operating an FBO. It covers aircraft in your care, custody or control, a gap that standard liability policies typically exclude. Airfield operators should also review [airport liability insurance](/qa/airport-liability-insurance/), and businesses with a product or parts exposure should see [aviation products liability insurance](/qa/aviation-products-liability-insurance/).

content.title: Shared Hangars and Partnerships
content.text: If two co-owners or club members share a hangar, decide in writing whose policy responds if one member's tug damages another member's airplane. Read [aircraft partnership insurance](/qa/aircraft-partnership-insurance/), and remember that many aircraft policies limit claims between people insured under the same policy.
What Airport Hangar Leases Typically Require

items: Minimum liability limits, often $1M, sometimes on a smooth basis (see [smooth vs per-seat liability](/compare/smooth-liability-vs-per-seat-sublimit-aircraft-insurance/)).
Proof of aircraft hull insurance.
An endorsement naming the airport authority as an [additional insured](/learn/named-insured-vs-additional-insured/).
Indemnification clauses. Have your broker confirm that your policy's contractual liability cover matches what you sign.
Annual certificates of insurance. Missing one can cost you your hangar.

content.text: Building a homebuilt in the hangar? Builder's risk and contents cover interact, as explained in [experimental aircraft insurance](/learn/experimental-aircraft-insurance/). Storing drones and cameras? See [drone insurance](/learn/drone-insurance/). After any hangar loss, follow [aircraft insurance claims: what to expect](/learn/aircraft-insurance-claims-what-to-expect/). The hangar-vs-tie-down premium difference is part of [airplane insurance cost](/learn/airplane-insurance-cost/).

articles.title: Light Sport Aircraft Insurance After MOSAIC: What Sport Pilots and LSA Owners Need to Know in 2026
articles.description: Light sport aircraft insurance after the FAA MOSAIC rule: what sport pilots can fly, S-LSA vs E-LSA cover, ultralights, and the questions to ask at renewal.
articles.author: Insurance Bhaiya Research Desk
keyTakeaways: The FAA's **MOSAIC** rule expanded sport pilot privileges on **October 22, 2025**, and replaced the old LSA definition with a performance-based light-sport category on **July 24, 2026**.
Sport pilots can now fly airplanes with up to a **59-knot stall speed** (clean), **four-seat** airframes (one passenger only), and, with endorsements, retractable gear and constant-speed props.

Insurers have said cover continues for sport pilots flying within their FAA privileges, but **conditions may be added case by case at renewal**. Disclose any new aircraft type to your insurer before flying it.
Factory-built **S-LSA** and kit-built **E-LSA** are underwritten differently. E-LSA follows many [experimental aircraft insurance](/learn/experimental-aircraft-insurance/) rules.

faqs.question: Can a sport pilot get insurance for a four-seat airplane after MOSAIC?
faqs.answer: Possibly, if the aircraft meets the 59-knot clean stall limit and the insurer's pilot warranty is satisfied. Expect make-and-model training requirements. See [aircraft & aviation insurance explained](/learn/aircraft-aviation-insurance-explained/).

faqs.question: Is light sport aircraft insurance cheaper?
faqs.answer: Usually, because hull values are lower. The hull rate and pilot-experience factors work the same way as for certified aircraft.

faqs.question: Can you insure a Part 103 ultralight?
faqs.answer: Yes, but the market is small and cover is often liability only.

content.text: Light sport aviation has always been the cheaper way into flying: a driver's license instead of a medical certificate, 20 hours minimum training for an airplane, and lighter, simpler aircraft. The FAA's MOSAIC rule has now expanded what counts as light sport and what a sport pilot can fly. Insurance terms are adjusting to those changes. This spoke of our [aircraft & aviation insurance explained](/learn/aircraft-aviation-insurance-explained/) hub covers what has changed and what hasn't.
What MOSAIC Changed

rows: 1,320 lb max gross (1,430 seaplane), 45-kt stall, 120-kt max
Performance-based: up to 61 KCAS stall (flaps), 250 KCAS max, no weight limit (from July 24, 2026)
Up to 59 KCAS clean stall; four-seaters with one passenger (from Oct 22, 2025)
Fixed gear, fixed-pitch or ground-adjustable prop
Retractable gear and constant-speed props with endorsements

content.title: New Privileges ≠ Automatic Coverage
content.text: Being legal to fly an older four-seat Cessna as a sport pilot doesn't mean your insurer will cover you in it. The pilot warranty still sets minimum hours and time in type. Tell your insurer before flying any aircraft type you haven't flown before. For Cessna-specific pricing, see [Cessna insurance](/qa/cessna-insurance/). Any change of aircraft or pilot should be added by [insurance endorsement](/learn/what-is-an-insurance-endorsement/), not just a phone call.
S-LSA vs E-LSA vs Ultralight Insurance

items: **S-LSA (special, factory-built):** Can be used for rental and flight training. Underwritten much like certified trainers, with standard hull and liability.

**E-LSA (experimental, kit- or plans-built):** Limited to sport, recreation and instruction of the owner. Underwriters look at build quality and documentation, as covered in [experimental aircraft insurance](/learn/experimental-aircraft-insurance/).
**Part 103 ultralights:** No FAA pilot certificate or aircraft registration is required, and fewer insurers write them. Cover is often liability only, sometimes through ultralight associations.

content.text: Hull is still written at an agreed value. Light sport aircraft have lower values than four-seat certified singles, so total premiums are usually lower too. The rate mechanics are the same as in [airplane insurance cost](/learn/airplane-insurance-cost/). The details of what hull cover pays are in [what does aircraft hull insurance cover](/qa/what-does-aircraft-hull-insurance-cover/). Sport pilots who rent should still carry [private pilot insurance](/qa/private-pilot-insurance/), and those sharing an LSA should read [aircraft partnership insurance](/qa/aircraft-partnership-insurance/). Light sport seaplanes have their own water-operation risks. See [seaplane insurance](/learn/seaplane-insurance/).

content.title: Flying on a Driver's License? Plan for Medical Changes
content.text: Sport pilots don't need an FAA medical, but life and disability underwriters will still ask about aviation. See [does life insurance cover private pilots](/qa/does-life-insurance-cover-private-pilots/) before you apply for a new life policy.

articles.title: Helicopter Insurance: Why Rotorcraft Cost About 2% of Hull a Year and How to Qualify for Better Rates
articles.description: Helicopter insurance explained: hull rates around 2% of value, R22 to Bell 206 premiums, the 1,000-hour / 100-in-type benchmark, and training credits of 10–20%.
articles.author: Insurance Bhaiya Research Desk
keyTakeaways: Helicopter hull premiums average around **2% of insured hull value** a year for experienced pilots, roughly double the rate for a fixed-gear piston airplane.
Indicative premiums: **Robinson R22 (~$300k hull) $4,000–$8,000**, **Bell 206 (~$1.5M) $15,000–$40,000** a year.
Preferred rates typically need **1,000+ total hours, 100+ in make and model**, and recurrent training every 12 months.
Approved manufacturer training courses can earn **10–20% premium discounts**.

faqs.question: Why is helicopter insurance more expensive than airplane insurance?
faqs.answer: Higher accident frequency, costly dynamic components and fewer insurers. Hull rates average around 2% of value against roughly 1% for piston airplanes. See the [aircraft & aviation insurance explained](/learn/aircraft-aviation-insurance-explained/) hub.

faqs.question: How much is insurance for a Robinson R22?
faqs.answer: Roughly $4,000–$8,000 a year on a ~$300,000 hull, depending on pilot hours, training and use.

faqs.question: How can I lower my helicopter insurance premium?
faqs.answer: Build make-and-model time, complete approved manufacturer training (10–20% credits), fly private rather than commercial missions, and keep a claim-free record.

content.text: Helicopters use the same insurance structure as airplanes: agreed-value hull plus liability, governed by a pilot warranty. The price is very different, though. This spoke of our [aircraft & aviation insurance explained](/learn/aircraft-aviation-insurance-explained/) hub explains why rotorcraft cost more to insure and how owners bring premiums down.
How Much Is Helicopter Insurance?

Compare those figures with the 0.9–1.3% hull rate on a typical piston airplane in our [airplane insurance cost](/learn/airplane-insurance-cost/) guide. Higher loss frequency, expensive dynamic components (rotor blades, gearboxes and so on) and a small pool of insurers all push rotorcraft rates up. Commercial, utility and air-medical missions cost substantially more than private flying. Underwriters score each rotorcraft pilot individually, as explained in [what is insurance underwriting](/learn/what-is-insurance-underwriting/), so two R44 owners can get very different quotes.
What Underwriters Want From Helicopter Pilots

items: **Total time:** 1,000+ hours for preferred rates. Low-time pilots pay more and may be offered higher deductibles.
**Make and model time:** 100+ hours in type is a common benchmark.
**Recurrent training:** Certified training every 12 months, with manufacturer courses earning 10–20% credits.
**Use:** Private and business use is cheapest. Instruction, tours, utility and EMS work are rated much higher.

content.title: Training Ownership: Instructors and Clubs
content.text: If you instruct in helicopters you don't own, you need your own non-owned liability policy. See [flight instructor insurance](/qa/flight-instructor-insurance/). Sharing ownership to split a $5,000+ premium? Read [aircraft partnership insurance](/qa/aircraft-partnership-insurance/) first, so that every partner is a named insured.
Coverage Points Unique to Helicopters

Check how the policy treats ground-running and hover-taxi damage (in motion or not in motion), external-load or sling operations (usually excluded unless scheduled), and off-airport landings. The general rules on what hull cover does and doesn't pay are in [what does aircraft hull insurance cover](/qa/what-does-aircraft-hull-insurance-cover/). Liability limits should be smooth rather than per-seat where possible (see [smooth vs per-seat liability](/compare/smooth-liability-vs-per-seat-sublimit-aircraft-insurance/)). Helicopter pilots also pay among the highest aviation flat extras on life insurance. See [does life insurance cover private pilots](/qa/does-life-insurance-cover-private-pilots/). Under the FAA's MOSAIC changes, sport pilots can now fly certain helicopters with simplified flight controls. See [light sport aircraft insurance](/learn/light-sport-aircraft-insurance/).

articles.title: Drone Insurance in 2026: Is It Required, What $1M Liability Costs, and Why DJI Care Isn't Insurance
articles.description: Drone insurance explained: no FAA mandate, Minnesota's rule, $500–$1,500 a year for $1M liability, hourly cover, hull rates and the homeowners trap.
articles.author: Insurance Bhaiya Research Desk
keyTakeaways: No US federal rule requires drone insurance for recreational or Part 107 commercial pilots. **Minnesota** is the exception: it requires commercial operators to carry an annual policy.
Clients set the real requirement. Contractors, brokerages and venues routinely ask for a certificate showing **$1M third-party liability**.
Typical 2026 pricing: **$500–$1,500 a year** for $1M commercial liability, or about **$10–$25 an hour** on demand. Hull cover runs about **8–12% of the drone's value** a year.
DJI Care Refresh is a replacement plan, **not insurance**. It never pays for the car, window or person your drone hits.

faqs.question: Do I need insurance to fly a drone under Part 107?
faqs.answer: Not under federal law. Minnesota requires commercial operators to carry insurance, and most clients will demand a $1M liability certificate. See the wider [aircraft & aviation insurance](/learn/aircraft-aviation-insurance-explained/) overview.

faqs.question: How much is drone liability insurance?
faqs.answer: About $500–$1,500 a year for $1M of annual commercial liability, or roughly $10–$25 an hour for on-demand cover.

faqs.question: Is DJI Care Refresh the same as drone insurance?
faqs.answer: No. It replaces your damaged drone for a fee but provides no liability cover and can't produce an insurance certificate.

content.text: Drones are aircraft in the eyes of the FAA, and most insurers treat them the same way: separate cover for the aircraft itself (hull) and for damage you cause to others (liability). This spoke of our [aircraft & aviation insurance explained](/learn/aircraft-aviation-insurance-explained/) hub covers what's legally required, what clients will ask you for, and what cover actually costs.
Is Drone Insurance Required?

items: **Federal (FAA):** No insurance mandate for recreational flyers or Part 107 commercial pilots. The FAA requires registration, Remote ID and, for recreational flyers, the TRUST test.
**Minnesota:** Requires commercial drone operators to carry insurance, and pay-per-flight cover doesn't satisfy the rule.

**Clients and venues:** The de facto mandate. Expect requests for a certificate of insurance with $1M liability, often with the client named as an [additional insured](/learn/named-insured-vs-additional-insured/).

content.text: How Much Does Drone Insurance Cost?

Drone hull rates of 8–12% are far higher than the 0.9–1.3% charged on piston airplanes (see [airplane insurance cost](/learn/airplane-insurance-cost/)), because drones crash, fly away and get dropped far more often. For a $2,000 drone, self-insuring the hull and buying only liability is often the better value. Run the numbers with the [Deductible Breakeven Calculator](/deductible-calculator/).

content.title: The Homeowners Business-Use Trap
content.text: A homeowners policy may cover liability from purely recreational drone flying, but any business use (even one paid real-estate shoot) typically voids that route. Some homeowners and umbrella policies also carry aircraft [exclusions](/learn/what-is-an-exclusion-in-insurance/). Read your policy's wording before relying on it, and see our [umbrella insurance](/learn/umbrella-insurance-guide/) guide for how aircraft exclusions work.
Insuring a Drone Business Properly

A drone business usually needs three layers. The first is aviation liability for the flights themselves. The second is equipment cover for drones, cameras and batteries in transit, often written as an inland marine floater (see [inland marine insurance explained](/learn/inland-marine-insurance-explained/)). The third is [commercial general liability](/learn/commercial-general-liability-guide/) for the business premises and operations. Store expensive kit in a hangar or workshop? Read [aircraft hangar insurance](/learn/aircraft-hangar-insurance/) for how contents cover works. If a flight goes wrong, the claims steps in [aircraft insurance claims: what to expect](/learn/aircraft-insurance-claims-what-to-expect/) apply to drones too. Moving up to crewed aircraft? Start with [private pilot insurance](/qa/private-pilot-insurance/) or the new sport-pilot options in [light sport aircraft insurance](/learn/light-sport-aircraft-insurance/).

articles.title: Full-Time RV Insurance: What Full-Timer Coverage Adds, and Why a Vacation RV Policy Isn't Enough When the RV Is Home
articles.description: Living in your RV? Full-timer coverage adds home-style liability and medical payments a vacation RV policy lacks. What it covers, domicile issues and gaps.
articles.author: Insurance Bhaiya Research Desk
keyTakeaways: A standard RV policy assumes you have a fixed home; full-timer coverage fills the liability and medical payments gap a homeowners policy would normally cover.
Full-timer liability applies to many incidents away from the RV, not only around the vehicle.
Your premium and legal minimums are set by your domicile state, not where you happen to be parked.
Not telling the insurer the RV is your only home can put claims at risk.
Pair full-timer coverage with replacement-cost or agreed-value physical damage and strong personal effects limits.

faqs.question: What is full-timer RV insurance?
faqs.answer: Coverage added to an RV policy for people who live in their RV, providing personal liability and medical payments similar to a homeowners policy.

faqs.question: Do I need full-timer coverage if I live in my RV part of the year?
faqs.answer: Insurers usually define full-time use by whether the RV is your primary residence. If you still own a home with homeowners insurance, you may not need it; ask the insurer for its definition.

faqs.question: Which state's insurance rules apply to full-time RVers?
faqs.answer: Generally your domicile state, where the RV is registered and you hold your license, though you must also meet the minimums of states you drive through.

faqs.question: Is full-time RV insurance expensive?
faqs.answer: It adds cost over a vacation policy, but it replaces liability protection you would otherwise lose when you sell your home. See [California RV insurance](/learn/california-rv-insurance/) for typical cost drivers.

content.text: Selling the house and living on the road changes your insurance more than most new full-timers expect. The homeowners policy that quietly covered your liability, your belongings and guest injuries is gone, and a vacation-use RV policy wasn't designed to replace it. This spoke builds on our [California RV insurance guide](/learn/california-rv-insurance/) and the broader [state auto insurance compliance guide](/learn/state-auto-insurance-compliance-guide/).
Vacation RV Policy vs Full-Timer Coverage

rows: Broader personal liability, similar to homeowners
Liability away from the RV (e.g., your dog bites someone at a park)
Higher limits available; essential when everything you own is aboard
Designed for RV as primary residence

content.title: Disclose Full-Time Use
content.text: If you tell the insurer the RV is a weekend vehicle but you live in it, a large liability or contents claim can be investigated as a misrepresentation. Tell the insurer it is your primary residence and buy the right coverage.
Your Domicile State Sets the Rules

Full-timers still need a legal domicile for registration, licensing and insurance. Many choose states known for full-timer services, including Florida. If your domicile is Florida, the legal minimum is PIP and property damage liability, not bodily injury, which is far too thin for a heavy motorhome; see [Florida minimum car insurance requirements](/qa/florida-minimum-car-insurance-requirements/). If you register in California, the motorhome needs 30/60/15 and you must show proof on demand; see [California evidence of liability insurance](/learn/california-evidence-of-liability-insurance/).
Coverage Checklist for Full-Timers

items: **Full-timer personal liability and medical payments.**
**High auto liability limits**, plus an [umbrella policy](/learn/umbrella-insurance-guide/) if you have savings to protect.
**Replacement-cost or agreed-value physical damage** so a total loss doesn't pay a depreciated [actual cash value](/glossary/actual-cash-value/).
**Personal effects** at a limit that matches everything you own.
**Emergency expense** for lodging when the RV is in the shop; you have no other home to go to.
**RV-specific roadside assistance.**
**Coverage for anything you tow.** A trailer or car behind the motorhome has its own gaps; see [does car insurance cover a travel trailer](/qa/does-car-insurance-cover-travel-trailer/).

content.title: Run a Gap Check Before You Sell the House
content.text: Before cancelling your homeowners policy, list every risk it covered and confirm each one is handled by the new RV policy. Our [8-Point Policy Check](/policy-check/) is a quick way to do it.
Health, Mail and Other Practicalities

Your domicile also affects [health insurance](/insurance/health-insurance/) networks, vehicle inspections and jury duty, so choose it deliberately. Insurance-wise, the key is consistency: the address on your license, registration and policy should match your declared domicile.

articles.title: California Low Cost Auto Insurance Program: Who Qualifies, What the 10/20/3 Policy Covers, and How to Apply
articles.description: California's Low Cost Auto program gives income-eligible drivers legal liability coverage. Eligibility, the 10/20/3 limits, gaps to know and how to apply.
articles.author: Insurance Bhaiya Research Desk
keyTakeaways: The California Low Cost Auto Insurance Program (CLCA) is a real state program, created under Insurance Code section 11629.7 and administered by the California Automobile Assigned Risk Plan.
Eligibility: household income at or below 250% of the federal poverty level, a vehicle worth $25,000 or less, age 16 or older, a valid California license and a good driving record.
CLCA policies carry 10/20/3 liability, below the regular 30/60/15 minimum, but they are legal evidence of financial responsibility for enrolled drivers.
CLCA covers injuries and damage you cause to others, not your own car.
Apply at mylowcostauto.com, by phone at 1-866-602-8861, or through a certified agent.

faqs.question: Who qualifies for low cost auto insurance in California?
faqs.answer: Drivers 16 or older with a valid California license, household income at or below 250% of the federal poverty level, a vehicle worth $25,000 or less, and a good driving record.

faqs.question: Is California low cost auto insurance legal coverage?
faqs.answer: Yes. Although its 10/20/3 limits are below the standard 30/60/15, it is valid evidence of financial responsibility for enrolled drivers.

faqs.question: Does CLCA cover damage to my own car?
faqs.answer: No. The base policy is liability only. Physical damage coverage is a separate decision; see [comprehensive vs collision](/compare/comprehensive-vs-collision/).

faqs.question: How do I apply for the California Low Cost Auto program?
faqs.answer: Visit mylowcostauto.com, call 1-866-602-8861, or find a certified agent. You will need proof of income, your license and vehicle details.

content.text: California's minimum liability rose to 30/60/15 in 2025, and for many lower-income drivers the price of staying legal rose with it. The state's answer is a genuine program, not an ad: the California Low Cost Auto Insurance Program. Unlike the 'program' marketing Florida drivers run into (see [Florida compliant drivers program](/learn/florida-compliant-drivers-program/)), this one is written into state law. It is part of the compliance picture laid out in our [state auto insurance compliance guide](/learn/state-auto-insurance-compliance-guide/).
Who Qualifies

rows: At or below 250% of the federal poverty level
Valid California driver's license (drivers with less than 3 years' experience became eligible in 2015)
Must meet the program's good driver definition

content.text: What a CLCA Policy Covers

The base policy is liability only: $10,000 for injury or death to one person, $20,000 per accident, and $3,000 for property damage. Those limits are lower than the regular 30/60/15 minimum, but for enrolled drivers they count as valid evidence of financial responsibility, which is what police and the DMV check (see [California evidence of liability insurance](/learn/california-evidence-of-liability-insurance/)). Additional coverage is available for an extra charge.

content.title: Legal, but Thin
content.text: $3,000 in property damage won't cover most bumper-and-headlight repairs on a newer car, and nothing in the base policy pays for your own vehicle. CLCA keeps you legal and avoids registration suspension; it does not make a crash affordable. Read [what happens if you crash without insurance](/qa/what-happens-if-you-crash-without-insurance/) to see how excess judgments are collected.
How to Apply

items: Check eligibility and get a quote at mylowcostauto.com or by calling 1-866-602-8861.
Gather proof of household income (such as tax returns or benefit letters), your license and vehicle details.
Complete the application online or with a certified CLCA agent near you.
Once the policy is issued, keep the ID card on paper or your phone; it is your proof at traffic stops.

content.text: Why Staying Insured Matters More Than the Price

Driving uninsured in California can mean a ticket of a few hundred dollars after penalty assessments (see [what happens if you can't show proof of insurance in California](/qa/california-no-proof-of-insurance-ticket/)). After an accident, it can mean a license suspension of up to four years, with an SR-22 filing to get it back, as explained in [do you have to report an accident to the California DMV](/qa/california-sr1-accident-report/). A CLCA policy costs far less than either outcome.

articles.title: Florida Mature Driver Insurance Discount: How Drivers 55+ Can Cut Premiums for Three Years With One Course
articles.description: Florida drivers 55 and older can earn an insurance discount by taking a state-approved mature driver course. Who qualifies, how long it lasts and how to claim it.
articles.author: Insurance Bhaiya Research Desk
keyTakeaways: Drivers 55 and older qualify for Florida's mature driver discount by completing an FLHSMV-approved course, typically a 6-hour course available online.
The discount is authorized by Section 627.0652, Florida Statutes, and typically lasts three years.
You keep it by avoiding at-fault crashes and moving violations during that period.
The size of the discount is set by each insurer, so ask for the figure before you enroll.
This is the genuine state-backed discount; ads for a 'compliant drivers program' are not.

faqs.question: How much is the Florida senior driver insurance discount?
faqs.answer: Florida law authorizes the discount, but each insurer sets the amount. Ask your insurer for its percentage before taking the course.

faqs.question: How long does the Florida mature driver discount last?
faqs.answer: Typically three years, provided you avoid at-fault crashes and moving violations. Retake the course to renew it.

faqs.question: Can I take the Florida mature driver course online?
faqs.answer: Yes. Many FLHSMV-approved providers offer it online. Confirm the provider is on the state's approved list before paying.

faqs.question: Is this the same as the Florida compliant drivers program?
faqs.answer: No. The mature driver course is authorized by Florida law. 'Compliant drivers program' is a marketing phrase; see our [Florida compliant drivers program](/learn/florida-compliant-drivers-program/) breakdown.

companionTool.title: Car Insurance Coverage Calculator
companionTool.description: Audit your automotive coverage checklist across liability, collision, comprehensive, and medical defense layers.

content.text: Florida has one discount that is actually written into state law, and most eligible drivers never claim it. If you are 55 or older, a single approved course can lower your premium for about three years. It is the real version of what 'state program' ads promise, as we explain in our [Florida compliant drivers program](/learn/florida-compliant-drivers-program/) guide, and it is one of the discounts covered in our [state auto insurance compliance guide](/learn/state-auto-insurance-compliance-guide/).
Who Qualifies

items: **Age:** 55 or older.

**Course:** Completion of a mature driver discount course from a provider approved by the Florida Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles (FLHSMV). Most providers offer it online as a roughly 6-hour self-paced course.
**Record:** To keep the discount for the full period, avoid at-fault crashes and moving violations.
**Policy:** A Florida auto policy with a participating insurer. The discount applies to your premiums; the amount is up to each insurer.

content.text: How to Claim It, Step by Step

items: **Call your insurer first** and ask what percentage it gives for a mature driver certificate, and which coverages it applies to.
**Choose an FLHSMV-approved provider.** The FLHSMV website lists approved mature driver courses; avoid any provider that isn't on it.
**Complete the course** and download your completion certificate.

**Send the certificate to your insurer** and confirm the discount appears on your next declarations page; our guide on [how to read an insurance policy](/learn/how-to-read-an-insurance-policy/) shows where discounts are listed.
**Set a reminder for three years** so you can retake the course before the discount expires.

content.title: Stack It With Other Real Discounts
content.text: The mature driver discount combines with multi-policy, paid-in-full and safe-driver discounts. Retirees who also own an RV can often bundle it; see [California RV insurance](/learn/california-rv-insurance/) if you travel west in winter.
Which Coverages It Helps

The statute targets the core premium components: liability, personal injury protection and collision. PIP is a required coverage in Florida, so a discount on it lowers the cost of staying legal; see [Florida PIP insurance explained](/learn/florida-pip-insurance-explained/) for what that coverage actually pays, and [Florida minimum car insurance requirements](/qa/florida-minimum-car-insurance-requirements/) for the full list of what you must carry.

content.title: Don't Trade Coverage for a Discount
content.text: Retirees on fixed incomes are often tempted to drop to Florida's bare minimum. With no bodily injury liability, one serious crash can put retirement savings at risk. If your savings exceed your liability limits, consider an [umbrella policy](/learn/umbrella-insurance-guide/).

content.description: Check whether your liability limits protect your retirement savings before deciding where to apply discount savings.

articles.title: Florida PIP Insurance Explained: The 14-Day Rule, the $2,500 Cap, and What Personal Injury Protection Really Pays
articles.description: Florida PIP explained: 80% of medical bills up to $10,000, the 14-day treatment rule, the $2,500 non-emergency cap, lost wages, and gaps PIP never covers.
articles.author: Insurance Bhaiya Research Desk
keyTakeaways: Florida PIP pays 80% of reasonable medical expenses and 60% of lost income, sharing one $10,000 limit, plus a separate $5,000 death benefit.
You must get initial medical treatment within 14 days of the crash or PIP can deny the claim entirely.
Without a diagnosed emergency medical condition, medical benefits are capped at $2,500, not $10,000.
PIP pays regardless of fault, but it never pays for vehicle damage or pain and suffering.
To sue the at-fault driver for pain and suffering, your injury must meet Florida's serious-injury threshold.

faqs.question: What is the 14-day rule for PIP in Florida?
faqs.answer: You must receive initial medical treatment within 14 days of the accident to use your PIP benefits. Treatment after that window can be denied.

faqs.question: Why did PIP only pay $2,500?
faqs.answer: PIP medical benefits are capped at $2,500 unless a qualifying provider diagnoses an emergency medical condition. With that diagnosis, the full $10,000 limit is available.

faqs.question: Does Florida PIP cover my car?
faqs.answer: No. PIP covers injuries and lost income only. Your car is covered by collision or comprehensive, and others' property by your property damage liability; see [Florida minimum car insurance requirements](/qa/florida-minimum-car-insurance-requirements/).

faqs.question: Can I sue the other driver in Florida?
faqs.answer: For pain and suffering, only if your injury meets the serious-injury threshold, such as permanent injury, significant scarring or disfigurement, or death. Economic losses beyond PIP may also be claimed from the at-fault driver.

content.text: [PIP](/glossary/personal-injury-protection/) is the coverage Florida drivers pay for every month and understand least. It is half of the state's legal minimum, alongside property damage liability, as covered in [what is the minimum car insurance required in Florida](/qa/florida-minimum-car-insurance-requirements/). It is also built around deadlines and caps that can shrink a $10,000 benefit to a fraction of that if you don't know them. This spoke of our [state auto insurance compliance guide](/learn/state-auto-insurance-compliance-guide/) explains exactly how it works.
What PIP Pays

rows: Up to $10,000 (or $2,500 without an emergency medical condition)
Covered only by property damage liability, collision or comprehensive
Only recoverable from the at-fault driver if the serious-injury threshold is met

content.text: The Two Rules That Cut PIP Benefits

items: **The 14-day rule.** You must receive initial treatment within 14 days of the crash. Miss it, and PIP can deny the claim entirely, even if pain shows up later. Get checked the same week, even if you feel fine.

**The emergency medical condition (EMC) rule.** The full $10,000 is available only if a qualifying provider (such as a physician, osteopath, dentist or physician assistant) documents an emergency medical condition. Without that diagnosis, medical benefits stop at $2,500.

content.title: The Most Expensive Week After a Crash
content.text: Skipping a doctor visit because you feel 'just sore' is the most common way Florida drivers lose PIP. Symptoms of whiplash and concussion often appear days later. Treatment inside 14 days protects the claim; treatment on day 15 may not.
Who PIP Covers

Your PIP covers you and resident relatives in your household, whether in your car, [someone else's car](/qa/can-i-add-someone-elses-car-to-my-insurance/), or hit as a pedestrian or cyclist. Passengers without their own PIP are generally covered by the PIP on the vehicle they were riding in. Because PIP pays regardless of fault, your own insurer handles your medical bills first, then any remaining claim goes against the at-fault driver.
The Gaps PIP Leaves

With 80% coinsurance-style reimbursement and a $10,000 ceiling, a single emergency room visit with imaging can consume much of the benefit. Insurers also offer PIP deductibles, which lower your premium but reduce what PIP pays. Pick a [deductible](/glossary/deductible/) you could actually afford after a crash. Optional medical payments coverage can pick up some of the 20% PIP doesn't pay, and bodily injury liability protects you when you are the one who causes injuries; neither is required, as our [Florida compliant drivers program](/learn/florida-compliant-drivers-program/) guide explains.

content.title: Lower Your PIP Cost Legitimately
content.text: Drivers 55 and older can complete a state-approved course to earn a discount on PIP, liability and collision premiums for about three years. See the [Florida mature driver insurance discount](/learn/florida-mature-driver-insurance-discount/) guide.
Don't Let PIP Lapse

Because PIP is a legal requirement, a cancellation is reported to the state and suspends your license and plate. See [what happens if car insurance lapses in Florida](/qa/what-happens-if-car-insurance-lapses-in-florida/) for the fees and how to reinstate.

articles.title: Seaplane Insurance: Floats, Amphibians, Water Landings and the Costs Land Pilots Never See
articles.description: Seaplane insurance explained: float vs amphibian pricing, SES experience underwriters want, wreck-removal costs, mooring gaps and 5–10% hull deductibles.
articles.author: Insurance Bhaiya Research Desk
keyTakeaways: Underwriters weigh **seaplane time** above everything else, then time in type, amphibian time (if insuring an amphib) and total time.
**Amphibians cost more to insure than straight floats** because retractable gear adds the risk of a gear-down water landing, which often flips the aircraft.
Hull deductibles on seaplanes commonly run **5%–10% of hull value**, and floats are typically covered as a separately scheduled part of physical damage.
Wreck removal can cost **tens of thousands of dollars** and may be legally required whatever the salvage value. Confirm that your policy has a dedicated limit for it.

faqs.question: Is seaplane insurance more expensive than regular airplane insurance?
faqs.answer: Generally yes. Water operations, wreck-removal exposure and the gear risk on amphibians push hull pricing and deductibles above the same airframe on wheels. Seaplane-specific time is the biggest discount lever. See the [aircraft & aviation insurance explained](/learn/aircraft-aviation-insurance-explained/) hub for the fundamentals.

faqs.question: Are floats covered under hull insurance?
faqs.answer: Usually yes, as a separately scheduled part of physical damage cover, for example $50,000 of a $300,000 hull value. Confirm that float theft is included.

faqs.question: Does seaplane insurance cover damage while the plane is docked?
faqs.answer: Not-in-motion cover usually applies, but wind and wave damage to docked or beached seaplanes can be limited depending on the policy wording. Ask your broker to confirm in writing.

companionTool.title: Insurance Needs Calculator
companionTool.description: Calculate your total protection requirement across life, health, and personal liability.

content.text: Seaplane insurance covers the same two building blocks as any aircraft policy, hull and liability, but water changes how losses happen and how much they cost. A sunk airframe has to be recovered from the lake bed, a docked floatplane can be wrecked by a storm without ever moving, and a single gear-position error can flip an amphibian on landing. This is a spoke of our [aircraft & aviation insurance explained](/learn/aircraft-aviation-insurance-explained/) hub.
What Underwriters Look At Before Quoting a Seaplane

items: **Seaplane (SES) time:** The most important factor. A 2,000-hour land pilot with 10 hours on floats is still a low-time seaplane pilot.

**Time in type:** Hours in the specific make and model, such as a Cessna 185 on floats or a Super Cub on amphibs. Cessna airframes on floats follow the same logic as our [Cessna insurance](/qa/cessna-insurance/) pricing, but with water-operation loadings added.
**Amphibian time:** Required separately if you're insuring an amphibian, because gear management is the key risk.
**Total time, ratings and recurrent training:** Seaplane-specific recurrent training is viewed favorably.

content.text: Straight Floats vs Amphibians: Why the Gear Matters

Straight floats only operate from water, so the pilot never has to manage landing gear. Amphibious floats add retractable wheels so the aircraft can use runways too. The trade-off is the risk of landing on water with the wheels down, which typically flips the aircraft, or landing on a runway with them up. Amphibious gear is also expensive to repair. As a result, amphibians are priced higher than the same airframe on straight floats, and insurers may require amphibian-specific dual instruction.

content.title: Wreck Removal Can Cost More Than the Airplane Is Worth
content.text: Raising a sunk floatplane can cost tens of thousands of dollars, and authorities can require removal whatever the aircraft's salvage value. Check that your policy has a wreck-removal or salvage limit separate from the hull value. Otherwise, a total loss can leave you paying for the recovery yourself. Boat owners face the same issue. See [boat insurance claims: what to expect](/learn/boat-insurance-claims-what-to-expect/).
Docked, Moored and Beached: The Not-in-Motion Gap

Standard not-in-motion hull cover was written with hangars and tie-downs in mind. Depending on the policy wording, damage from wind or waves to a **docked or beached seaplane** may be limited or excluded, and some policies exclude superficial hail damage that doesn't affect airworthiness. Read the wording carefully, using our guide to [what an exclusion is in insurance](/learn/what-is-an-exclusion-in-insurance/). If you swap between wheels and floats seasonally, some policies require the change to be scheduled with the insurer in advance.
Typical Seaplane Policy Structure

rows: Upgrade to smooth limits if you carry passengers. See [smooth vs per-seat](/compare/smooth-liability-vs-per-seat-sublimit-aircraft-insurance/)
Aircraft value, with floats as a scheduled part (e.g. $300,000 total, $50,000 for floats)
Separate float theft and damage limit
Occupants injured in a water landing
Can exceed hull value on deep-water losses

content.text: With a 5%–10% deductible, a $200,000 floatplane leaves you responsible for the first $10,000–$20,000 of any hull loss. That [deductible](/glossary/deductible/) has to sit in your emergency fund, not on a credit card. For general premium context, see [airplane insurance cost](/learn/airplane-insurance-cost/). If you're building a float-equipped kitplane, also read [experimental aircraft insurance](/learn/experimental-aircraft-insurance/).

content.title: Get Your Rating on a Rented Floatplane First
content.text: Most pilots earn the SES rating in a school's floatplane. Carry [private pilot insurance](/qa/private-pilot-insurance/) that explicitly covers non-owned seaplanes, because some renter policies exclude amphibians or water operations. Then build hours before buying. Our [first-airplane scenario](/scenarios/brian-first-cessna-182-texas/) shows how hours in type move a quote.

If the worst happens on the water, follow the NTSB and insurer steps in [aircraft insurance claims: what to expect](/learn/aircraft-insurance-claims-what-to-expect/), and confirm the wreck-removal limit before you call a salvage company. Float operations also raise aviation flat extras on life insurance (see [does life insurance cover private pilots](/qa/does-life-insurance-cover-private-pilots/)). Instructors giving SES training need their own cover, explained in [flight instructor insurance](/qa/flight-instructor-insurance/). Docked-aircraft gaps are explained further in [what does aircraft hull insurance cover](/qa/what-does-aircraft-hull-insurance-cover/).

articles.title: Experimental Aircraft Insurance: Covering a Homebuilt From First Rivet to Phase I and Beyond
articles.description: Experimental aircraft insurance explained: builder's risk, Phase I fly-off limits, 10% in-motion deductibles and insuring a used homebuilt.
articles.author: Insurance Bhaiya Research Desk
keyTakeaways: An amateur-built aircraft needs **three different policies** over its life: builder's risk (ground, not in motion), a restricted Phase I fly-off policy, and a normal flight policy.

During the FAA fly-off period (40 hours, or 25 with a certificated engine/propeller combination), **no passengers are allowed**, liability may be capped near $500,000, and in-motion hull deductibles of **10%** are common.
Builder's risk typically values your labor at **factory-estimated build hours × a standard hourly wage**, not shop rates. Keep receipts and a build log.
Many insurers will not cover a first flight at all. Line up your insurer, and any transition training it requires, before the airworthiness inspection.

faqs.question: Can you get insurance for an experimental aircraft?
faqs.answer: Yes, but from fewer insurers and with stricter terms: builder's risk during construction, a restricted Phase I policy and then normal cover. Start with the overview in [aircraft & aviation insurance explained](/learn/aircraft-aviation-insurance-explained/).

faqs.question: Does experimental aircraft insurance cover passengers during Phase I?
faqs.answer: No. The FAA prohibits passengers during the fly-off period, and Phase I policies typically exclude passenger liability. Passenger cover returns after Phase I, usually with a per-seat sublimit.

faqs.question: How is the hull value of a homebuilt decided?
faqs.answer: It is set as an agreed value supported by build receipts, the build log and often an independent appraisal. During construction, labor is usually valued at standard build hours times a standard hourly wage.

content.text: Experimental aircraft insurance is the hardest corner of general aviation to insure. Each homebuilt is effectively a one-of-one aircraft with limited claims data, and fewer insurers write them. This spoke of our [aircraft & aviation insurance explained](/learn/aircraft-aviation-insurance-explained/) hub follows a kitplane from the build to its first flight and on to resale, and shows where the [premium](/glossary/premium/) and the restrictions change.
Stage 1: Builder's Risk While the Aircraft Is Under Construction

While the airplane is in your garage or hangar, you need **ground not-in-motion** hull cover, often called builder's risk. It covers fire, theft, windstorm and damage to parts in storage or in transit. It does not cover taxiing or flight. As the build progresses, an *aircraft under construction* [endorsement](/learn/what-is-an-insurance-endorsement/) raises the insured value. Insurers usually reimburse labor at factory-estimated build hours times a standard hourly wage rather than a professional shop rate, so your build log is your proof of loss. Check whether your [home insurance](/learn/home-insurance-fundamentals/) covers aircraft parts in a home workshop at all. Many policies exclude aircraft and aircraft parts entirely.

content.title: Don't Wait Until the Airframe Is Finished
content.text: A garage fire 1,500 hours into a build can destroy $80,000+ of kit, engine and avionics. Buy builder's risk as soon as you've invested meaningful money, and update the declared value at major milestones such as the engine arriving or the panel being installed.
Stage 2: Phase I Flight Testing (the Fly-Off)

After the FAA issues the special airworthiness certificate, the aircraft must complete a test period, typically **40 hours**, or **25 hours** when a certificated engine and propeller combination is used. During this period no passengers may be carried. Insurers respond with a restricted policy:

items: **Liability capped** at around $500,000 with **no passenger liability**, since passengers are prohibited anyway.

**In-motion hull deductible of about 10%** of the agreed value. On a $100,000 airplane, that means you absorb the first $10,000 of any taxi or flight damage. Weigh that [deductible](/glossary/deductible/) against your cash reserves.
**Named test pilot only**, often with required dual instruction in a similar type: 5–20 hours is typical for tailwheel or retractable designs, and much more for turbine conversions.
**Some insurers decline first-flight risk entirely.** In that case, fly Phase I on ground-only cover and accept the hull risk yourself, or use a carrier that specializes in homebuilts.

content.text: Stage 3: Normal Operations After Phase I

Once Phase I is signed off, the insurer converts the policy to normal flight cover. Passenger liability returns, though usually with a **$100,000 per-seat [sublimit](/glossary/sub-limit/)**. Smooth $1M limits or $250,000-per-seat options are hard to find for custom-built aircraft. Our [smooth liability vs per-seat sublimit](/compare/smooth-liability-vs-per-seat-sublimit-aircraft-insurance/) comparison explains why that gap matters. Hull is written at an **agreed value**, which for a homebuilt should be backed by build receipts or an independent appraisal. That protects you from the depreciation haircut built into [actual cash value](/glossary/actual-cash-value/) settlements.
Buying a Used Experimental Aircraft

Second owners face tougher underwriting than original builders. The insurer is relying on someone else's workmanship. Expect requests for the build log, a recent condition inspection by an experienced inspector, and transition training in type. Get an insurance quote before you sign the purchase agreement. An airplane you can't insure at a sensible price is worth much less to you. The same buy-side discipline applies to certified aircraft, as [Brian's first Cessna 182 scenario](/scenarios/brian-first-cessna-182-texas/) shows. For general pricing context on certified aircraft, compare with our [airplane insurance cost](/learn/airplane-insurance-cost/) guide and [Cessna insurance](/qa/cessna-insurance/) benchmarks.

rows: Labor valued at standard build hours

content.title: Floats on a Homebuilt?
content.text: Amphibious and float-equipped kitplanes combine two specialty risks, and insurers are especially selective about them. Read [seaplane insurance](/learn/seaplane-insurance/) before you specify floats. If you plan to fly from rented aircraft while your build is underway, carry [private pilot insurance](/qa/private-pilot-insurance/) in the meantime.

content.title: Kit-Built Light Sport, Shared Builds and Workshops
content.text: Kit-built E-LSA aircraft fall under both these rules and the post-MOSAIC changes in [light sport aircraft insurance](/learn/light-sport-aircraft-insurance/). Building with partners? Settle named-insured status early, using [aircraft partnership insurance](/qa/aircraft-partnership-insurance/). Building in a rented hangar? Check the building and contents split in [aircraft hangar insurance](/learn/aircraft-hangar-insurance/). Builder's risk is pure not-in-motion cover, explained in [what does aircraft hull insurance cover](/qa/what-does-aircraft-hull-insurance-cover/).

A $100,000 Cessna 172 flown by an experienced private owner usually costs **$1,200–$2,500 a year**. A low-time pilot pays **$2,000–$3,500+** for the same airplane.
Renter's (non-owned) cover runs about **$60–$100 a year** for liability only and **$175–$400** with physical damage.

Upgrading from a $100,000 per-seat sublimit to smooth liability adds cost but closes the biggest gap in most policies. See [smooth vs per-seat liability](/compare/smooth-liability-vs-per-seat-sublimit-aircraft-insurance/).

faqs.question: How much does airplane insurance cost per year?
faqs.answer: For most privately owned piston singles, expect hull value × 0.9%–1.3% plus $300–$1,200 for liability, which comes to roughly $1,200–$2,500 a year for a $100,000 Cessna 172 with an experienced owner. Renters pay about $175–$400 a year. See the [aircraft & aviation insurance explained](/learn/aircraft-aviation-insurance-explained/) hub for how the coverages fit together.

faqs.question: How much is aircraft insurance for a Cessna?
faqs.answer: A Cessna 172 usually costs $1,100–$2,500 a year depending on the pilot, and a published broker example for a 1979 Cessna 182 came in at about $1,450. Retractable models like the 210 cost more. Full breakdown: [Cessna insurance](/qa/cessna-insurance/).

faqs.question: How much is aviation insurance for a jet?
faqs.answer: A light Citation jet with a $5M hull typically costs $10,000–$25,000 a year, with $5M–$10M smooth liability and strict type-rating and simulator-training requirements.

faqs.question: Is liability-only aircraft insurance cheaper?
faqs.answer: Yes. Owners of older, low-value aircraft sometimes drop hull cover and keep liability only, usually a few hundred dollars a year. Do this only if you can absorb a total loss of the airframe yourself, and check whether a lender or hangar lease requires hull cover.

content.text: Airplane insurance cost is driven far more by **the pilot** than by the airplane. Two owners of identical Cessnas can receive quotes $1,500 apart because one has 1,200 hours and an instrument rating and the other has 90 hours and a new private certificate. This guide is a spoke of our [aircraft & aviation insurance explained](/learn/aircraft-aviation-insurance-explained/) hub. It shows how insurers build the price, what real 2026 quotes look like, and which levers actually move your [premium](/glossary/premium/).
How Much Does Airplane Insurance Cost? The Two-Part Formula

Most owner policies are priced in two parts. The hull premium is a rate applied to the agreed hull value: **0.9% to 1.3% a year** for typical piston aircraft, according to published broker guides. Liability is priced separately: about **$300 to $600 a year** for piston aircraft at standard limits, rising to $1,200 for higher or smooth limits. Then the underwriter adjusts for pilot hours, ratings, recency, retractable gear, hangar or tie-down storage and claims history, the same risk scoring we explain in [what is insurance underwriting](/learn/what-is-insurance-underwriting/).

content.title: Worked Example: $100,000 Cessna 172
content.text: Hull: $100,000 × 1.1% = **$1,100**. Liability ($1M with $100k per seat): **≈ $450**. Total ≈ **$1,550 a year** for an experienced owner with the aircraft hangared. The same airplane with a 75-hour pilot can price above $3,000, because the hull rate climbs much faster than the liability charge. Model-by-model numbers are in our [Cessna insurance](/qa/cessna-insurance/) answer.
How Much Is Aircraft Insurance by Aircraft Type?

Specialty categories sit outside this table. Float and amphibian aircraft carry water-specific risks and larger deductibles (see [seaplane insurance](/learn/seaplane-insurance/)), and homebuilts have a narrower insurer market with restricted cover during flight testing (see [experimental aircraft insurance](/learn/experimental-aircraft-insurance/)).
How Much Is Plane Insurance If You Don't Own a Plane?

If you rent from a flight school or fly a friend's airplane, you buy **non-owned aircraft** (renter's) insurance instead of an owner's policy. Typical 2026 pricing is **$60–$100 a year** for liability only, **$175–$400** once you add physical damage to the rented aircraft, and **$300–$500** for student pilots. Our [private pilot insurance](/qa/private-pilot-insurance/) answer explains why the school's own policy doesn't protect you.
How Much Is Aviation Insurance for a Low-Time Pilot?

Low-time owners pay the most, and in some cases are offered no hull cover at all until they complete dual instruction in the aircraft. Expect a requirement of 5–15 hours with a CFI in make and model, a higher in-motion [deductible](/glossary/deductible/), and a premium of $2,000–$3,500+ on a $100,000 trainer. Rates fall noticeably once you pass roughly 250–500 total hours and add an instrument rating. For a step-by-step example, follow [Brian's first Cessna 182 scenario](/scenarios/brian-first-cessna-182-texas/).

content.title: The Cheapest Quote Often Has the Thinnest Liability
content.text: Two quotes that both say '$1M liability' can differ by a $100,000 per-seat [sub-limit](/glossary/sub-limit/). Compare quotes coverage by coverage using [how to compare insurance policies](/learn/how-to-compare-insurance-policies/), not premium against premium. Remember that your [umbrella insurance](/learn/umbrella-insurance-guide/) almost certainly excludes aircraft.

Other aircraft types follow very different math: [helicopter insurance](/learn/helicopter-insurance/) runs around 2% of hull value, [drone insurance](/learn/drone-insurance/) 8–12%, and [light sport aircraft insurance](/learn/light-sport-aircraft-insurance/) is usually cheaper because hull values are lower. Splitting the bill with co-owners? See [aircraft partnership insurance](/qa/aircraft-partnership-insurance/). Not sure what the hull part of the premium actually buys? Read [what does aircraft hull insurance cover](/qa/what-does-aircraft-hull-insurance-cover/). Hangaring the aircraft lowers the premium but adds building exposures; see [aircraft hangar insurance](/learn/aircraft-hangar-insurance/).

articles.title: Aircraft & Aviation Insurance Explained: Hull, Liability, Pilot Warranties and What It Really Costs
articles.description: How aircraft insurance works: hull vs liability, smooth vs per-seat limits, pilot warranties, and real 2026 costs for owners, renters and homebuilders.
articles.author: Insurance Bhaiya Research Desk
keyTakeaways: Aircraft insurance has two main parts: **hull** (damage to your plane, usually insured at an agreed value) and **liability** (injury or damage you cause to passengers and third parties). See the full [airplane insurance cost](/learn/airplane-insurance-cost/) breakdown.

A privately owned Cessna 172 with a $100,000 hull and $1M liability typically costs about **$1,200–$2,500 a year** in 2026. Low-time pilots pay $2,000–$3,500+ ([Cessna insurance](/qa/cessna-insurance/)).

Per-seat passenger sublimits (often $100,000 a seat) are the most underestimated gap in general aviation. Compare [smooth liability vs per-seat sublimits](/compare/smooth-liability-vs-per-seat-sublimit-aircraft-insurance/) before you sign.
The **pilot warranty** decides whether any claim pays. If the person flying doesn't meet the named-pilot or open-pilot requirements, coverage can be void, even for an unrelated accident.

Renting? The flight school's policy protects the flight school, not you. [Private pilot insurance](/qa/private-pilot-insurance/) (non-owned/renter's cover) costs roughly $175–$400 a year with physical damage.

faqs.question: How much is aviation insurance for a small private plane?
faqs.answer: For a typical four-seat piston single such as a Cessna 172 with a $100,000 hull and $1M liability, expect roughly $1,200 to $2,500 a year if you're an experienced pilot and $2,000 to $3,500+ if you're low-time. Liability-only cover costs considerably less. See the worked examples in our [airplane insurance cost](/learn/airplane-insurance-cost/) guide.

faqs.question: Is aircraft insurance required by law?
faqs.answer: The FAA doesn't require private Part 91 aircraft owners to carry liability insurance. However, lenders require hull coverage, most hangar leases and airports require liability coverage, some states set their own rules, and commercial operators face separate federal requirements. Uninsured flying puts your personal assets at risk, because personal [umbrella insurance](/glossary/umbrella-insurance/) usually excludes aircraft.

faqs.question: Do I need insurance if I only rent planes?
faqs.answer: Yes. The FBO's policy protects the FBO. If you damage a rental, its insurer can recover the cost from you through subrogation. Non-owned aircraft cover is inexpensive. See [private pilot insurance](/qa/private-pilot-insurance/).

faqs.question: Why is experimental or seaplane insurance harder to get?
faqs.answer: Fewer insurers write these risks, accident data is thinner, and water operations add salvage and wreck-removal costs. Expect stricter pilot requirements and higher deductibles. Read [experimental aircraft insurance](/learn/experimental-aircraft-insurance/) and [seaplane insurance](/learn/seaplane-insurance/).

faqs.question: Does life insurance cover pilots who die in a plane crash?
faqs.answer: It can, if aviation isn't excluded. Insurers may charge a flat extra of roughly $2.50–$10 per $1,000 or offer an aviation exclusion rider instead. See [does life insurance cover private pilots](/qa/does-life-insurance-cover-private-pilots/).

content.text: Aviation insurance doesn't work like car insurance. There is no standard state-mandated form and no comparison site with instant quotes. The FAA doesn't require private Part 91 owners to carry liability coverage, although lenders, hangar leases, airports and some states do. Every policy is underwritten individually by a small group of specialist aviation insurers, and the price depends mostly on **who is flying** rather than what is flying. This hub explains how the pieces fit together and links to our deep-dive guides on [airplane insurance cost](/learn/airplane-insurance-cost/), [Cessna insurance](/qa/cessna-insurance/), [private pilot insurance](/qa/private-pilot-insurance/), [experimental aircraft insurance](/learn/experimental-aircraft-insurance/) and [seaplane insurance](/learn/seaplane-insurance/).
The Two Building Blocks: Hull Coverage and Liability Coverage

Every owner's aircraft policy is built from two main coverages plus optional add-ons. Before you compare quotes, you need to know which of these coverages each quote actually includes, the same discipline we teach in [how to compare insurance policies](/learn/how-to-compare-insurance-policies/).

rows: Damage while parked, tied down or hangared: hail, windstorm, hangar fire, vandalism, theft
Every owner, including during annuals and storage

Owners with financed or high-value aircraft
Injury or death to passengers and people on the ground, damage to property

content.text: Hull Coverage: Why Agreed Value Matters

Most aircraft hulls are insured on an **agreed value** basis: you and the insurer fix a value at policy inception and that is what a total loss pays, less any [deductible](/glossary/deductible/). That is very different from [actual cash value](/glossary/actual-cash-value/), where the adjuster subtracts depreciation after the loss. The same trade-off applies to classic boats, as we explain in [agreed value vs actual cash value boat insurance](/compare/agreed-value-vs-actual-cash-value-boat-insurance/). Insure for too little and you lose the difference on a total loss. Insure for too much and you pay a higher premium every year for value you could never collect.
Liability Coverage: Smooth Limits vs Per-Seat Sublimits

A policy advertised as '$1 million liability' often pays only **$100,000 per passenger**. That per-seat cap is a [sub-limit](/glossary/sub-limit/). A 'smooth' or combined single limit lets the full $1M go to whoever is injured. If one passenger suffers a catastrophic injury, the difference between the two can be $900,000 of personal exposure. We break this down line by line in [smooth liability vs per-seat sublimit aircraft insurance](/compare/smooth-liability-vs-per-seat-sublimit-aircraft-insurance/), and it ties directly to the broader lesson in [coverage vs limits](/learn/coverage-vs-limits/).

content.title: Your Umbrella and Homeowners Policies Will Not Catch a Plane Crash
content.text: Standard homeowners policies and most personal umbrella policies **exclude aircraft liability**. If your aviation policy's per-seat sublimit runs out, there is usually no second layer behind it. Read the aircraft exclusion in your own [umbrella insurance](/learn/umbrella-insurance-guide/) before you assume you're protected, and see [what an exclusion means in insurance](/learn/what-is-an-exclusion-in-insurance/).
The Pilot Warranty: The Clause That Decides Whether Any Claim Pays

Aviation policies contain a **pilot warranty** (also called the pilot clause) listing who may fly the aircraft. Usually that is a short list of named pilots and an 'open pilot' clause, such as: *any pilot holding a private certificate with 500 total hours and 25 hours in make and model*. If someone who doesn't meet those requirements is at the controls, the insurer can deny the claim, even if their lack of experience had nothing to do with the accident. Read this section of your policy closely, using our guide on [how to read an insurance policy](/learn/how-to-read-an-insurance-policy/).

items: **Named pilot requirements:** Certificates, ratings and hours exactly as listed. A named pilot who lets their flight review or medical lapse can fall outside coverage.
**Airworthiness:** Flying with an expired annual inspection or an unresolved airworthiness directive can void hull coverage.
**Use of aircraft:** A 'pleasure and business' policy does not cover flights for hire. Charging passengers can turn a covered flight into an excluded one.
**Medical certification:** Confirm in writing that your insurer accepts BasicMed if you fly under it.
**Changes mid-term:** Adding a pilot or changing use requires an [insurance endorsement](/learn/what-is-an-insurance-endorsement/). Don't rely on a phone call.

content.title: Lenders Need a Breach-of-Warranty Endorsement
content.text: If your aircraft is financed, the lender will require a lienholder or breach-of-warranty endorsement so it gets paid even if you breach the pilot warranty. That endorsement protects the bank's collateral, not you. You can still owe the full loan balance on a destroyed airplane. Understand who is protected by reading [named insured vs additional insured](/learn/named-insured-vs-additional-insured/).
How Much Is Aviation Insurance? A 2026 Snapshot

Piston aircraft hull premiums typically run about **0.9% to 1.3% of the insured hull value per year**, plus $300 to $1,200 for liability, according to published broker rate guides. Pilot experience, retractable gear, high performance, hangar vs tie-down storage and claims history then move that number up or down. Our full [airplane insurance cost](/learn/airplane-insurance-cost/) guide shows the worked math. The table below gives indicative ranges.

Market is narrower; Phase I limits apply

content.text: Which Aviation Policy Fits You?

items: **You rent from an FBO or flight school:** You need non-owned aircraft (renter's) cover. The school's insurer can pursue you for damage through [subrogation](/glossary/subrogation/). Start with [private pilot insurance](/qa/private-pilot-insurance/).

**You're buying your first certified single:** Read [Cessna insurance](/qa/cessna-insurance/) for model-by-model pricing, then follow [Brian's first Cessna 182 scenario](/scenarios/brian-first-cessna-182-texas/) to see how a low-time owner gets an insurable quote.

**You're building or buying a homebuilt:** You'll need builder's risk during construction and a restricted policy during Phase I flight testing. See [experimental aircraft insurance](/learn/experimental-aircraft-insurance/).
**You fly floats or an amphibian:** Water operations add wreck-removal costs, mooring risk and the gear-down water landing risk. See [seaplane insurance](/learn/seaplane-insurance/).

**You carry friends or family:** Decide between per-seat and smooth limits using our [smooth liability vs per-seat sublimit](/compare/smooth-liability-vs-per-seat-sublimit-aircraft-insurance/) comparison.

content.text: Aviation Businesses: Airports and Manufacturers

Owner and renter policies cover the operation of an aircraft. Businesses that operate airfields or make aircraft parts face a different risk and buy different cover. See [airport liability insurance](/qa/airport-liability-insurance/) for premises exposure at airfields and FBOs, and [aviation products liability insurance](/qa/aviation-products-liability-insurance/) for manufacturers and parts suppliers. Because so few carriers write aviation risk, most policies are placed through specialist brokers. Our [agent vs broker vs insurer](/learn/agent-vs-broker-vs-insurer/) guide explains who works for whom, and [what is insurance underwriting](/learn/what-is-insurance-underwriting/) explains why your logbook matters more than your credit score here.

content.title: Five Moves That Lower Aviation Premiums
content.text: 1) Get an instrument rating or log recurrent training. Many insurers give credits for it. 2) Hangar the aircraft instead of tying it down. 3) Accumulate time in make and model before you upgrade to a complex aircraft. 4) Set an agreed hull value that matches realistic market value. 5) Get quotes through a broker who has access to multiple aviation markets, and review the result with our [8-Point Policy Check](/policy-check/).
More Aviation Insurance Guides
Aviation risk goes beyond owning a single-engine airplane. Use these guides for every other part of flying:

items: **What hull cover pays:** [What does aircraft hull insurance cover](/qa/what-does-aircraft-hull-insurance-cover/), including in-motion vs not-in-motion cover, agreed value and the exclusions.
**Rotorcraft:** [Helicopter insurance](/learn/helicopter-insurance/), with hull rates around 2% of value and the 1,000-hour benchmark.
**Sport flying after MOSAIC:** [Light sport aircraft insurance](/learn/light-sport-aircraft-insurance/) for S-LSA, E-LSA and ultralights.
**Unmanned aircraft:** [Drone insurance](/learn/drone-insurance/), covering Part 107, $1M liability costs and why DJI Care isn't insurance.
**Shared ownership:** [Aircraft partnership insurance](/qa/aircraft-partnership-insurance/) for co-owners and flying clubs.
**Teaching:** [Flight instructor insurance](/qa/flight-instructor-insurance/) for independent CFIs.
**Where you park it:** [Aircraft hangar insurance](/learn/aircraft-hangar-insurance/), covering the building, contents and hangarkeepers liability.
**When things go wrong:** [Aircraft insurance claims: what to expect](/learn/aircraft-insurance-claims-what-to-expect/), including NTSB Part 830 reporting.
**Protecting your family:** [Does life insurance cover private pilots](/qa/does-life-insurance-cover-private-pilots/), with flat extras and aviation exclusion riders explained.
**Protecting your income:** [Pilot loss of license insurance](/qa/pilot-loss-of-license-insurance/) for professional pilots.
