glossary.whyItMatters: Discovering an inner sub-limit on high-value jewelry, bicycles, musical instruments, or specialized hospital surgeries only after a catastrophe occurs is one of the most painful and common consumer insurance surprises.

miniQuiz.question: You own a $7,000 watch. Your home policy has a $150,000 contents limit and a $1,500 jewelry theft sub-limit. If the watch is stolen, how much will the policy pay (ignoring deductible)?

options.text: $7,000 in full because your overall contents limit is $150,000.
options.explanation: Incorrect. The specific category sub-limit overrides the general policy limit for that item.

options.text: $1,500, the maximum allowable under the jewelry sub-limit.
options.explanation: Exactly right! Sub-limits restrict payouts for specific loss categories regardless of how large the overall policy limit is.

options.text: $0 because jewelry is an uninsurable personal hazard.
options.explanation: Incorrect. It is covered, but strictly capped at the sub-limit.

options.text: Half of the watch's depreciated actual cash value.
options.explanation: Incorrect. The sub-limit is a firm dollar cap on the payout.

faqs.question: How can I protect my jewelry and collectibles above standard sub-limits?
faqs.answer: You can add a 'Scheduled Personal Property Endorsement' (also called an insurance floater or rider). You submit a certified appraisal, and the insurer covers the item for its full agreed value with zero deductible and no sub-limit.

faqs.question: Are sub-limits common in health insurance policies?
faqs.answer: Yes. Many international, travel, and supplementary private health plans impose sub-limits on room and board charges (e.g., $500/day maximum), physical therapy sessions (e.g., $1,000/year cap), or prescription medications.

glossary.title: What Is Insurance Discovery? Definition & How It Protects Patients
glossary.description: Insurance discovery is how healthcare providers find a patient's active coverage when it wasn't reported or was incomplete, preventing an unnecessary self-pay bill.
glossary.simpleDefinition: The process healthcare providers use to find a patient's active insurance coverage when it wasn't provided, was incomplete, or was thought to not exist at all.
glossary.scoutExplanation: [Insurance discovery](/glossary/insurance-discovery/) is mostly a provider-side, behind-the-scenes process rather than something a patient does themselves. When someone shows up at a hospital or clinic without insurance information — an unconscious emergency patient, someone who forgot their card, or someone who genuinely didn't realize they still had active Medicaid or a parent's plan covering them — billing offices run an insurance discovery search across multiple payer databases to find any billable coverage before writing the balance off as bad debt or billing the patient directly. It's different from ordinary eligibility verification, which just confirms whether a known policy is currently active; discovery works with limited information (name, date of birth, address) to find coverage nobody knew to check for.
glossary.example: Maria is brought to the ER unconscious after a car accident and can't provide any insurance information. The hospital's billing office runs an insurance discovery search using her name and date of birth, and finds that she's still covered under her employer's health plan from a job she started two weeks earlier — coverage she didn't even know had activated yet. The claim is billed correctly to that plan instead of becoming Maria's direct financial responsibility.
glossary.whyItMatters: For patients, insurance discovery working correctly is what stands between a medical bill going to your actual insurer versus landing on you personally as self-pay. If you've ever been surprised that a hospital found coverage you forgot you had, this is the process responsible — and it's also why keeping your insurance information current with providers reduces the risk of an unnecessary self-pay bill while discovery is still running its course. See [what does health insurance actually cover?](/learn/what-does-health-insurance-actually-cover/) for the broader coverage picture this process protects.

miniQuiz.question: What is the main difference between insurance discovery and standard eligibility verification?

options.text: They are the same process with different names
options.explanation: Not quite — verification checks a known policy, while discovery searches for coverage that isn't already on file.

options.text: Eligibility verification confirms a known policy is active; discovery searches for coverage nobody has reported yet
options.explanation: Exactly right. Verification is a lookup against a known payer; discovery is an exhaustive search when that information is missing or incomplete.

options.text: Discovery only applies to dental insurance
options.explanation: Incorrect. Insurance discovery is most commonly used in general medical and hospital billing, not limited to dental coverage.

options.text: Discovery is something only patients can request, not providers
options.explanation: Incorrect. Insurance discovery is almost always run by the provider's billing office or a third-party revenue-cycle vendor, not initiated by the patient.

content.text: Insurance discovery sits behind the scenes of nearly every hospital or clinic billing office, but it directly affects whether a patient's bill lands correctly on an insurer or incorrectly on the patient themselves.
How the Discovery Process Actually Works

When a patient's insurance information is missing, incomplete, or apparently non-existent, a provider's billing office runs a discovery search using limited identifying details — name, date of birth, address — against multiple payer databases simultaneously. This differs from routine eligibility verification, which simply confirms whether a policy the patient already reported is currently active. Discovery is used specifically when there's no known policy to check in the first place, most commonly for unconscious emergency patients, forgotten insurance cards, or coverage a patient didn't realize had recently activated.
Why This Matters Even If You Never See It Happen

If discovery finds active coverage, the claim gets billed to that payer instead of becoming the patient's direct financial responsibility or being written off as uncompensated care. Keeping your insurance information current with providers — even ones you don't visit often — shortens how long a bill might sit in limbo while a discovery search runs its course. See [what does health insurance actually cover?](/learn/what-does-health-insurance-actually-cover/) for the broader coverage picture this process protects.
This entry is educational and general in nature. Specific billing and insurance discovery practices vary by provider, health system, and revenue-cycle vendor.

glossary.title: What Is a PEO Health Plan? Definition & How Co-Employment Works
glossary.description: A PEO health plan pools employees from many small businesses under one master policy through co-employment, giving small employers large-group-style pricing and benefits.
glossary.simpleDefinition: A health plan offered through a Professional Employer Organization (PEO), which pools employees from many small businesses together under one master policy to access group rates closer to those of a large employer.
glossary.scoutExplanation: A [PEO health plan](/glossary/peo-health-plan/) works through what's called a co-employment arrangement: your business enters a contract with a PEO, which becomes the official 'employer of record' for HR, payroll, and benefits purposes, while your company keeps control of day-to-day work direction. Because the PEO combines employees from many client businesses into one large [risk pool](/learn/how-does-insurance-work/), even a five-person company can access benefits and pricing normally reserved for employers with hundreds of workers — a meaningfully different structure from a standard small-group policy purchased directly from a carrier, and from a [level-funded plan](/compare/level-funded-vs-fully-insured-health-insurance/), which stays entirely within one employer's own risk pool.
glossary.example: A 12-person marketing agency can't get competitive group health rates on its own. It partners with a PEO, which combines the agency's employees with those of hundreds of other small client businesses into one large pool, letting the agency offer employees a large-employer-style plan (often including better provider networks and lower per-employee costs) that it couldn't have accessed independently.
glossary.whyItMatters: If you're a small-business owner comparing benefits options, a PEO plan can meaningfully close the pricing and plan-quality gap with larger employers, but it also means giving up some administrative control since the PEO becomes your employees' legal employer for benefits purposes — and if your business ever leaves the PEO arrangement, you'll typically need to set up a new standalone plan rather than simply keeping the same policy. See [what does health insurance actually cover?](/learn/what-does-health-insurance-actually-cover/) for how PEO coverage compares on actual benefits.

miniQuiz.question: What makes a PEO health plan different from a standard small-group health policy?

options.text: PEO plans only cover Medicare-eligible employees
options.explanation: Incorrect. PEO plans are unrelated to Medicare eligibility and are used for working-age employees of small businesses.

options.text: The PEO pools employees from many small businesses into one large risk pool under co-employment
options.explanation: Correct. This pooling is what lets small employers access pricing and benefits closer to a large group plan.

options.text: A PEO plan is always more expensive than a direct small-group policy
options.explanation: Not necessarily — PEO pooling often lowers per-employee cost precisely because the risk pool is larger, though results vary by PEO and industry.

options.text: A PEO plan requires the business to become fully self-funded
options.explanation: Incorrect. The PEO, not the individual client business, holds the master policy and manages the funding structure.

content.text: A PEO health plan is one of the main ways a small business can access benefits and pricing that would otherwise only be realistic for a much larger employer.
The Co-Employment Structure, Explained

Entering a PEO arrangement means signing a co-employment contract: the PEO becomes the official 'employer of record' for payroll, tax filings, and benefits administration, while your business keeps full control over hiring, firing, and day-to-day work direction. Because the PEO combines employees from potentially hundreds of small client businesses into one large risk pool, even a very small company can access provider networks and per-employee pricing normally reserved for large employers.
How This Compares to Other Small-Business Options

A PEO plan is a structurally different path than a standard small-group policy or a [level-funded health plan](/compare/level-funded-vs-fully-insured-health-insurance/) — those keep your business as the sole legal policyholder, while a PEO plan sits under one much larger master policy shared across many employers. See [what does health insurance actually cover?](/learn/what-does-health-insurance-actually-cover/) and [Marcus's small business health plan structure scenario](/scenarios/marcus-small-business-health-plan-structure/) for how a real small employer weighs this decision.

content.title: What Happens If You Leave the PEO
content.text: If your business ever exits a PEO arrangement, you typically can't simply keep the same policy — you'll need to set up a new standalone group plan, which is worth planning for well before any transition.
This entry is educational and general in nature. PEO contract terms, benefits, and pricing structures vary significantly by provider and should be reviewed with a licensed benefits advisor.

glossary.title: What Is COBRA Continuation Coverage? Definition, Cost & Eligibility
glossary.description: COBRA lets you temporarily keep your employer's exact health plan after a qualifying event like job loss, by paying the full premium yourself plus a small admin fee.
glossary.simpleDefinition: A federal law letting you temporarily keep your employer's group health plan after leaving a job, by paying the full premium yourself, usually plus a small administrative fee.
glossary.scoutExplanation: [COBRA continuation coverage](/glossary/cobra-continuation-coverage/) is triggered by specific 'qualifying events' — voluntary or involuntary job loss (other than for gross misconduct), a reduction in work hours that ends benefits eligibility, divorce, a dependent aging out of coverage, or the covered employee's death. It applies to employers with 20 or more employees under the federal law (many states have a 'mini-COBRA' equivalent for smaller employers). The coverage itself is identical to what you had as an active employee — same network, same benefits — but you now pay the full [premium](/glossary/premium/) the employer used to subsidize, plus up to a 2% administrative fee, which is why COBRA premiums often come as a shock compared to the payroll-deducted amount you were used to seeing.
glossary.example: After being laid off, David elects COBRA to keep his family on the same health plan while job hunting. His premium jumps from the $180/month he used to see deducted from his paycheck to $850/month, because he's now paying the portion his employer used to cover plus his own share, plus a 2% administrative fee — but he keeps the exact same doctors and network without any gap in coverage.
glossary.whyItMatters: COBRA is rarely the cheapest option, but it's often the only way to keep the exact same doctors and coverage with zero gap after a qualifying event — comparing its actual cost against a marketplace plan (which a job loss also qualifies you for, via special enrollment) is worth doing before defaulting to COBRA automatically. See [level-funded vs. fully-insured health insurance](/compare/level-funded-vs-fully-insured-health-insurance/) and [PEO health plan](/glossary/peo-health-plan/) for how the employer-side plan structure you're leaving affects what continuation coverage actually looks like.

miniQuiz.question: Why do COBRA premiums typically feel much higher than what someone paid as an active employee?

options.text: COBRA plans always have worse benefits than the original employer plan
options.explanation: Incorrect. COBRA coverage is identical to the active-employee plan — same network and benefits, just a different cost structure.

options.text: The person now pays both their own share and the portion their employer used to subsidize, plus an admin fee
options.explanation: Correct. Employers typically cover a large share of premiums for active employees; COBRA removes that subsidy, so the full cost (plus up to 2%) falls on the individual.

options.text: COBRA always charges a higher rate than the market rate for the same plan
options.explanation: Incorrect. COBRA premiums reflect the plan's actual group cost plus a capped admin fee, not an inflated market rate.

options.text: COBRA is only available at premium, upgraded coverage tiers
options.explanation: Incorrect. COBRA simply continues the exact same plan the person already had — there's no tier upgrade involved.

content.text: COBRA is often misunderstood as a separate insurance product, when it's really a legal right to temporarily keep the exact plan you already had.
What Triggers COBRA Eligibility

COBRA applies after specific 'qualifying events': voluntary or involuntary job loss (other than for gross misconduct), a reduction in work hours that ends benefits eligibility, divorce, a dependent aging out of coverage, or the covered employee's death. It applies to employers with 20 or more employees under the federal law, and many states have a 'mini-COBRA' equivalent extending similar rights to employees of smaller employers.
Why the Premium Jumps So Much

Employers typically subsidize a large share of active employees' premiums. Under COBRA, that subsidy disappears — you pay the full premium the plan actually costs, plus up to a 2% administrative fee, which is why a COBRA bill often looks dramatically higher than what used to come out of a paycheck for the same exact coverage.
COBRA Isn't Your Only Option

Losing job-based coverage also opens a special enrollment window for an ACA marketplace plan, which — especially with income-based subsidies — can sometimes end up cheaper than COBRA for the same transition period. See [ACA marketplace plan vs. employer-sponsored health insurance](/compare/aca-marketplace-vs-employer-sponsored-health-insurance/) for a full side-by-side comparison before defaulting to COBRA automatically.

This entry is educational and general in nature and does not constitute legal advice. COBRA eligibility windows, costs, and state mini-COBRA rules vary; confirm your specific situation with your plan administrator or a benefits professional.

glossary.title: What Is Prior Authorization? Definition & Why Claims Get Denied Without It
glossary.description: Prior authorization is the approval an insurer requires before certain treatments, procedures, or medications are covered — skipping it is a leading cause of claim denials.
glossary.simpleDefinition: Approval your health insurer requires before it will pay for certain treatments, procedures, or medications — obtained before the care happens, not after.
glossary.scoutExplanation: [Prior authorization](/glossary/prior-authorization/) exists so insurers can review whether a specific treatment meets their medical necessity criteria before agreeing to pay for it, and it's most commonly required for expensive procedures (like bariatric surgery), higher levels of mental health care (like inpatient or residential treatment), certain specialty medications (including many GLP-1 weight-loss drugs), and imaging like [MRIs](/qa/how-much-does-an-mri-cost-without-insurance/) or [CT scans](/qa/how-much-is-a-ct-scan-with-insurance/). The request is typically submitted by your provider's office, not by you directly, but the outcome directly affects your wallet: skipping a required prior authorization is one of the most common reasons an otherwise legitimate claim gets denied outright, regardless of whether the care itself was medically appropriate.
glossary.example: Before scheduling bariatric surgery, Elena's surgeon's office submits a prior authorization request documenting her BMI, comorbidities, and prior weight-loss attempts. The insurer approves it in advance, confirming the surgery will be covered before Elena undergoes the procedure — if the office had skipped this step, the claim could have been denied afterward even though Elena met all the medical criteria.
glossary.whyItMatters: A denied prior authorization isn't necessarily the final word — most plans have a formal appeals process, and getting the plan's specific written medical policy criteria (not just the denial letter) is usually the fastest way to understand what additional documentation could change the outcome. See [does health insurance cover weight loss drugs or bariatric surgery?](/qa/does-health-insurance-cover-weight-loss-drugs-bariatric-surgery/) and [does health insurance cover therapy and mental health treatment?](/qa/does-health-insurance-cover-therapy-mental-health/) for two of the most common real-world prior authorization scenarios.

miniQuiz.question: What typically happens if a provider skips a required prior authorization before a procedure?

options.text: The claim is automatically covered since the procedure already happened
options.explanation: Incorrect. Skipping a required prior authorization is one of the most common reasons a claim is denied outright, regardless of medical necessity.

options.text: The claim is commonly denied, even if the treatment was medically appropriate
options.explanation: Correct. Prior authorization is a procedural requirement separate from medical necessity — missing it can result in denial even for appropriate care.

options.text: The patient automatically qualifies for a full refund from the provider
options.explanation: Incorrect. Skipping prior authorization affects insurance coverage, not the provider's billing obligations.

options.text: Prior authorization only applies to prescription drugs, not procedures
options.explanation: Incorrect. Prior authorization commonly applies to surgeries, imaging, higher levels of mental health care, and specialty medications alike.

content.text: Prior authorization is one of the most common reasons an otherwise medically appropriate claim gets denied — not because the care was wrong, but because a required approval step was skipped.
What Actually Requires Prior Authorization

Insurers typically require prior authorization for expensive or higher-risk categories of care: major surgeries like bariatric procedures, higher levels of mental health treatment such as inpatient or residential care, certain specialty medications including many GLP-1 weight-loss drugs, and advanced imaging like MRIs and CT scans. The request is almost always submitted by the treating provider's office, not the patient directly, and reviewed against the insurer's specific written medical necessity criteria before treatment happens.
Why Skipping It Is So Costly

A missing prior authorization is a procedural failure, separate from whether the underlying care was medically necessary — which is exactly why it can result in a full claim denial even for entirely appropriate treatment. See [does health insurance cover weight loss drugs or bariatric surgery?](/qa/does-health-insurance-cover-weight-loss-drugs-bariatric-surgery/) and [does health insurance cover therapy and mental health treatment?](/qa/does-health-insurance-cover-therapy-mental-health/) for two of the most common real-world scenarios where this comes up.

content.title: If You're Denied
content.text: Ask your insurer for their specific written medical policy criteria for that treatment, not just the denial letter — it's usually the fastest way to see exactly what documentation an appeal would need.
This entry is educational and general in nature. Prior authorization requirements vary by insurer, plan, state, and treatment type.

glossary.title: What Is Lay-Up Coverage? Seasonal Motorcycle Insurance Explained
glossary.description: Lay-up coverage (seasonal motorcycle insurance) keeps theft and fire cover on a stored bike while pausing riding coverages. How it works and what it saves.
glossary.simpleDefinition: Lay-up coverage is a seasonal option that keeps comprehensive protection (theft, fire, vandalism, storm damage) on a stored vehicle, usually a motorcycle, while suspending the riding coverages such as liability and collision until you ride again.
glossary.scoutExplanation: Think of lay-up coverage as putting your policy into hibernation rather than killing it. During the lay-up period, the coverages that only matter when you ride (liability, collision, and often UM/UIM and medical payments) are suspended, so you stop paying for them. Comprehensive stays active, because a bike sitting in a garage can still be stolen, catch fire or be crushed by a falling shelf. The [Insurance Information Institute](https://www.iii.org/article/motorcycle-insurance) describes these seasonal policies as mostly offered in northern states with real winters. The big advantage over cancelling is that there's **no coverage lapse**. A lapse can raise your next premium and leave the stored bike unprotected. See [what happens when insurance expires](/learn/what-happens-when-insurance-expires/). Lay-up is one of the easiest ways to lower the figures in our [average cost of motorcycle insurance](/learn/average-cost-of-motorcycle-insurance/) guide, and it works alongside the choices in [full coverage vs liability-only motorcycle insurance](/compare/full-coverage-vs-liability-only-motorcycle-insurance/).
glossary.example: Nicole rides her $11,000 cruiser in Ohio from April to October. Her full-coverage policy costs $540 a year, or $45 a month. She puts the bike on lay-up from November through March, five months, with comprehensive only at about $8 a month. The riding coverages she pauses would have cost about $37 a month, so she saves roughly $185 that year (5 × $37). When her garage is broken into in January, her comprehensive claim for the stolen bike is still paid, minus her $500 deductible.
glossary.whyItMatters: Riding a laid-up bike is the danger. If you take it out 'just once' on a warm February day and crash, there's usually no liability or collision coverage in force, which is effectively the same as [crashing without insurance](/qa/what-happens-if-you-crash-without-insurance/). Always reactivate the policy before you ride, and confirm the change in writing. And never cancel outright to save money. A stolen bike with no comprehensive in place is a total loss. Here's how theft claims pay out: [does motorcycle insurance cover theft](/qa/does-motorcycle-insurance-cover-theft/).

miniQuiz.question: Your motorcycle is on lay-up coverage for the winter. Which of these is still covered?

options.text: Your bike is stolen from your locked garage
options.explanation: Correct. Lay-up keeps comprehensive active, and comprehensive covers theft, fire and vandalism while the bike is stored.

options.text: You take the bike for a quick ride on a sunny day and hit a parked car
options.explanation: Not covered. Liability and collision are suspended during lay-up. You must reactivate the riding coverages before you ride.

options.text: Your friend borrows the bike and injures a pedestrian
options.explanation: Not covered. With liability suspended, injuries caused while riding a laid-up bike generally aren't covered.

options.text: All of the above, since the policy is still active
options.explanation: The policy is active, but only comprehensive is in force. That's why lay-up costs less.

content.text: Lay-Up Coverage vs Cancelling vs Pausing

**Lay-up** keeps comprehensive and your continuous-coverage history intact at a lower price. **Cancelling** saves a little more short-term, but it creates a lapse and leaves the bike unprotected, and some states' registration rules penalize lapses. **Pausing** is the car-insurance version of the same idea. See [can you pause car insurance](/qa/can-you-pause-car-insurance/). Lay-up also matters for financed bikes, because lenders require comprehensive to stay active. If you owe more than the bike is worth, read about [gap insurance](/glossary/gap-insurance/).
Who Should Use Lay-Up Coverage?

It suits riders in cold-winter states like Ohio, Colorado and the Northeast who store their bike for three months or more, owners of classic or summer-only bikes, and anyone laid up by injury or deployment. Check the cost in your state with [how much is motorcycle insurance in Ohio](/qa/how-much-is-motorcycle-insurance-in-ohio/) and [how much is motorcycle insurance in Colorado](/qa/how-much-is-motorcycle-insurance-in-colorado/), and find every related topic in the [motorcycle & powersport insurance hub](/learn/motorcycle-dirt-bike-powersport-insurance/).

Not every insurer offers lay-up, and the coverages suspended vary by insurer and state. Confirm the details in writing before storing your bike. Source: [Insurance Information Institute](https://www.iii.org/article/motorcycle-insurance).

glossary.title: What Is Custom Parts and Equipment Coverage? Motorcycle CPE Explained
glossary.description: Custom parts and equipment (CPE) coverage pays for aftermarket exhausts, seats, paint and luggage after theft or a crash. Learn the limits that apply.
glossary.simpleDefinition: Custom parts and equipment coverage pays to repair or replace aftermarket add-ons you've fitted to your motorcycle or vehicle, such as exhausts, seats, paint, luggage and electronics, when they're damaged or stolen in a covered loss, up to a dollar limit you choose.
glossary.scoutExplanation: A standard motorcycle policy values your bike as the manufacturer built it. Anything you add afterward (a $1,200 slip-on exhaust, a $900 custom seat, $2,500 of paint, hard luggage, a GPS) is covered only through custom parts and equipment coverage. It works as a [sub-limit](/glossary/sub-limit/) that sits on top of your collision and comprehensive coverage. Many policies include a small amount automatically, and you can buy more. The [Insurance Information Institute](https://www.iii.org/article/motorcycle-insurance) warns that standard policies often limit accessory coverage and advises checking your insurer's limits before you add upgrades. Losses are paid minus your [deductible](/glossary/deductible/), and often at depreciated [actual cash value](/glossary/actual-cash-value/) unless your policy says otherwise. This coverage decides how much you actually get back in a theft claim. See [does motorcycle insurance cover theft](/qa/does-motorcycle-insurance-cover-theft/). It also matters in a total loss, as the [financed motorcycle total-loss scenario](/scenarios/financed-motorcycle-totaled-owes-more-than-value/) shows.
glossary.example: Marcus's sport bike is worth $9,000 stock, and he's added $4,000 of parts: an exhaust, levers, a tail tidy and new bodywork. His policy includes $1,500 of CPE coverage and a $500 comprehensive deductible. When the bike is stolen, the insurer pays $9,000 + $1,500 − $500 = $10,000. Marcus loses $2,500 of upgrades he paid for. Raising his CPE limit to $4,000 would have added only a small amount to his annual premium.
glossary.whyItMatters: Under-declared modifications are one of the most common reasons riders feel short-changed after a claim. If you don't raise your CPE limit to match your receipts, you're self-insuring the difference. And if you fail to disclose major modifications such as performance tuning or derestricting, some insurers may treat it as misrepresentation, which can put the whole claim at risk. Keep receipts and photos, and update your limit every time you add a part. Compare with how [full coverage](/learn/car-insurance-guide/) protects the rest of the bike in [full coverage vs liability-only motorcycle insurance](/compare/full-coverage-vs-liability-only-motorcycle-insurance/).

miniQuiz.question: Your stolen motorcycle is worth $8,000 stock. You added $3,000 of aftermarket parts, your CPE limit is $1,000 and your deductible is $500. What does the insurer pay?

options.explanation: Correct. $8,000 (bike) + $1,000 (CPE limit) − $500 (deductible) = $8,500. The other $2,000 of parts is above your limit.
That would pay all $3,000 of parts. Upgrades are capped at your $1,000 CPE limit.
That ignores the $1,000 of CPE coverage you do have.
That ignores both the CPE limit and your deductible.

content.text: What Counts as Custom Parts and Equipment?

It typically includes aftermarket exhausts, seats, handlebars, levers, lighting, custom paint and graphics, chrome, fairings, saddlebags and luggage, sound systems, GPS units, sidecars and trailers, depending on the policy. Riding gear such as helmets and jackets is often a separate optional coverage. On ATVs, it covers winches, plows and racks. See [quad bike & ATV insurance](/learn/quad-bike-atv-insurance/). On dirt bikes it covers suspension upgrades and graphics. See [dirt bike insurance coverage](/learn/dirt-bike-insurance-coverage/).
How to Set the Right CPE Limit

Add up your receipts for every non-factory part, round up, and set your CPE limit at or above that total. Re-check it after every upgrade and at renewal. Store photos and receipts in the cloud, not on the bike. For how these choices move your premium, see [average cost of motorcycle insurance](/learn/average-cost-of-motorcycle-insurance/), and for the full coverage menu, visit the [motorcycle & powersport insurance hub](/learn/motorcycle-dirt-bike-powersport-insurance/).
Included CPE amounts, maximum limits and valuation methods vary by insurer. Check your declarations page. Source: [Insurance Information Institute](https://www.iii.org/article/motorcycle-insurance).

glossary.title: What Is Personal Injury Protection (PIP)? Definition, Coverage & Which States Require It
glossary.description: Personal injury protection (PIP) pays your medical bills and lost wages after a car crash, whoever caused it. What PIP covers and which states require it.
glossary.simpleDefinition: Personal injury protection (PIP) is car insurance that pays medical bills, part of your lost wages and related costs for you and your passengers after a crash, no matter who caused it. It's the core of 'no-fault' insurance.
glossary.scoutExplanation: PIP is first-party coverage: you claim on your own policy, not the other driver's. That's what makes it fast. There's no need to prove fault, so benefits usually start within weeks. It's mandatory in the 12 [no-fault states](/learn/no-fault-vs-at-fault-car-insurance-states/), where it replaces most small injury lawsuits. In return, your right to sue is limited by a [tort threshold](/glossary/tort-threshold/). Limits vary widely. New York requires $50,000 of basic economic loss cover, including lost earnings up to $2,000 a month ([NY Insurance Law §5102](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/ISC/5102)). Florida requires $10,000, and Texas insurers must offer it and include it unless you reject it in writing ([Texas OPIC](https://www.opic.texas.gov/auto-insurance/basics/)). PIP is broader than MedPay, which only covers medical bills. See [PIP vs MedPay](/compare/pip-vs-medpay/). Some things it doesn't do: PIP never pays for vehicle damage, and it doesn't cover the other driver's injuries. Your liability coverage handles those.
glossary.example: Maria lives in New York and is rear-ended on the way to work. Her ER visit, MRI and 10 weeks of physical therapy cost $14,000 at New York's fee-schedule rates, and she misses 6 weeks of work earning $4,500 a month. Her own PIP pays the $14,000 in medical bills and about $3,000 in lost wages ($2,000-a-month cap × 1.5 months), for about $17,000 in total. It starts paying within weeks, before anyone formally decides who caused the crash. Her car repairs are handled separately through the other driver's property damage liability.
glossary.whyItMatters: Getting PIP wrong usually means one of three things. First, missing the filing deadline: in New York it's 30 days, as explained in [how to file a no-fault insurance claim in New York](/qa/how-to-file-a-no-fault-insurance-claim-in-new-york/). Second, rejecting PIP in an at-fault state like [Texas](/qa/is-texas-a-no-fault-state/) and then waiting months for the other insurer. Third, carrying the bare minimum when your income depends on your health. And remember that motorcycles are commonly excluded from PIP systems, including in [New York](/learn/new-york-no-fault-insurance/) and Florida.

miniQuiz.question: You're injured in a crash in a no-fault state, and the other driver clearly caused it. Who pays your medical bills first?

options.text: Your own PIP coverage
options.explanation: Correct. In no-fault states your own PIP pays first, regardless of fault. You can pursue the at-fault driver only if you meet the tort threshold.

options.text: The at-fault driver's liability insurance
options.explanation: That's how at-fault states like Texas and Georgia work. In a no-fault state, your own PIP pays first.

options.text: Your collision coverage
options.explanation: Collision pays for your car, not your injuries.

options.text: Nobody, until a court decides fault
options.explanation: The whole point of PIP is that it pays quickly, without waiting for a fault decision.

content.text: Which States Require PIP?

PIP is required in Florida, Hawaii, Kansas, Kentucky, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, New York, North Dakota, Pennsylvania and Utah (the no-fault states), and in some other states as an add-on. Texas requires insurers to offer it. Colorado dropped PIP in 2003 and now defaults to $5,000 of MedPay instead. See [is Colorado a no-fault state](/qa/is-colorado-a-no-fault-state/). Georgia doesn't require PIP. See [is Georgia a no-fault state](/qa/is-georgia-a-no-fault-state/).
PIP and Health Insurance

In no-fault states, PIP generally pays before your health insurance for crash injuries. In some states you can coordinate the two to lower your premium. If you're weighing that trade-off, read [does health insurance cover car accidents and PIP](/qa/does-health-insurance-cover-car-accidents-pip/).

PIP limits, deductibles and eligibility rules vary by state and change over time. Sources: [NY Insurance Law §5102](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/ISC/5102), [Texas OPIC](https://www.opic.texas.gov/auto-insurance/basics/) and [ValuePenguin no-fault summary](https://www.valuepenguin.com/no-fault-auto-insurance).

glossary.title: What Is a Tort Threshold? Verbal vs Monetary Thresholds in No-Fault States
glossary.description: A tort threshold is the injury level you must reach in a no-fault state before you can sue the at-fault driver. Here's how verbal and monetary thresholds work.
glossary.ukTerm: No direct equivalent (the UK uses a fault-based system)
glossary.simpleDefinition: A tort threshold is the line you must cross in a no-fault state before you're allowed to sue the at-fault driver for pain and suffering. It's either a 'verbal' definition of serious injury or a 'monetary' amount of medical bills.
glossary.scoutExplanation: No-fault insurance makes a trade: your own [personal injury protection](/glossary/personal-injury-protection/) pays your bills quickly, and in exchange you give up the right to sue for minor injuries. The tort threshold is where that trade ends. **Verbal thresholds** list qualifying injuries. New York's 'serious injury' definition in [Insurance Law §5102(d)](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/ISC/5102) includes a fracture, significant disfigurement, permanent limitation of a body function, and being unable to perform your usual daily activities for 90 of the first 180 days. **Monetary thresholds** open the courthouse door once your medical bills pass a dollar figure, for example $2,000 in Kansas and Massachusetts or $4,000 in Minnesota ([ValuePenguin](https://www.valuepenguin.com/no-fault-auto-insurance)). **Choice no-fault** states (Kentucky, New Jersey and Pennsylvania) let you pay more to keep full tort rights, or less to accept a limited-tort threshold. At-fault states like [Texas](/qa/is-texas-a-no-fault-state/), [Georgia](/qa/is-georgia-a-no-fault-state/) and [Colorado](/qa/is-colorado-a-no-fault-state/) have no threshold at all. Compare the systems in [no-fault vs at-fault car insurance states](/learn/no-fault-vs-at-fault-car-insurance-states/).
glossary.example: Two New York drivers are rear-ended the same day. Derek has whiplash, needs 8 weeks of physical therapy and misses 3 weeks of work. His no-fault PIP pays his $6,500 in bills and his lost wages, but his injury doesn't meet the serious-injury threshold, so he can't sue for pain and suffering. Rita breaks her wrist. A fracture is a listed serious injury, so after PIP pays her bills she can also sue the at-fault driver for pain and suffering. Her claim later settles for $60,000 on top of her no-fault benefits.
glossary.whyItMatters: If you misunderstand your threshold, you can make two costly mistakes. You might settle too early, before doctors confirm a qualifying injury like a herniated disc with significant limitation. Or you might pick 'limited tort' in a choice state just to save on [premium](/glossary/premium/) without realising what rights you've given up. Always get a full medical workup and keep records that document limitation and missed days. The 90/180-day category in New York depends on proof. The claim steps are in [how to file a no-fault insurance claim in New York](/qa/how-to-file-a-no-fault-insurance-claim-in-new-york/).

miniQuiz.question: In a no-fault state with a verbal tort threshold like New York, which injury would most likely let you sue the at-fault driver for pain and suffering?

options.text: A fractured collarbone
options.explanation: Correct. A fracture is one of the listed 'serious injury' categories under NY Insurance Law §5102(d).

options.text: Bruising that heals in two weeks
options.explanation: Minor soft-tissue injuries usually don't meet a verbal threshold. PIP covers the bills, but you can't sue for pain and suffering.

options.text: Any injury, as long as the other driver was 100% at fault
options.explanation: That's the rule in at-fault states. In no-fault states, fault alone doesn't open the door to a lawsuit. The injury must meet the threshold.

options.text: Damage to your car over $10,000
options.explanation: Vehicle damage claims are always fault-based and aren't limited by the tort threshold. The threshold applies to injury claims.

content.text: Verbal vs Monetary Thresholds at a Glance

States with verbal thresholds include Florida, Michigan, New Jersey (limitation-on-lawsuit option), New York and Pennsylvania (limited tort). States with monetary thresholds include Hawaii, Kansas, Kentucky, Massachusetts, Minnesota, North Dakota and Utah. Monetary thresholds are easier to meet as medical costs rise, which is one reason some reform debates favour verbal thresholds. Read the full no-fault state list in our [no-fault vs at-fault hub](/learn/no-fault-vs-at-fault-car-insurance-states/), and see how New York applies its threshold in [New York no-fault insurance](/learn/new-york-no-fault-insurance/).

Threshold definitions and dollar amounts are set by state law and can change. This isn't legal advice. Sources: [NY Insurance Law §5102](https://www.nysenate.gov/legislation/laws/ISC/5102) and [ValuePenguin no-fault summary](https://www.valuepenguin.com/no-fault-auto-insurance).

glossary.title: What Is Comparative Negligence? Pure vs Modified Fault Rules by State
glossary.description: Comparative negligence reduces your car accident payout by your share of the fault. Learn pure vs modified (50% and 51%) rules and how your state splits blame.
glossary.ukTerm: Contributory negligence (UK term for reduced damages)
glossary.simpleDefinition: Comparative negligence is the legal rule that reduces how much you can recover after a crash by your own percentage of fault. If you were 30% to blame, your payout drops by 30%, and in some states, being too much at fault means you get nothing.
glossary.scoutExplanation: Most crashes aren't 100% one driver's fault, so insurers and courts assign percentages. States use one of four systems ([Bloomberg Law chart](https://pro.bloomberglaw.com/insights/litigation/contributory-and-comparative-negligence-by-state/)). **Pure comparative**: you recover something at any fault level, reduced by your share. California and New York use it. See [is California a no-fault state](/qa/is-california-a-no-fault-state/). **Modified, 51% bar**: you recover nothing at 51% or more. Texas uses it, as explained in [is Texas a no-fault state](/qa/is-texas-a-no-fault-state/). **Modified, 50% bar**: you recover nothing at 50% or more. Georgia and Colorado use versions of it. See [is Georgia a no-fault state](/qa/is-georgia-a-no-fault-state/) and [is Colorado a no-fault state](/qa/is-colorado-a-no-fault-state/). **Contributory negligence**: a handful of jurisdictions bar recovery if you're even 1% at fault. These rules matter most in at-fault states and in no-fault-state lawsuits that pass the [tort threshold](/glossary/tort-threshold/). The full picture is in our [no-fault vs at-fault car insurance states hub](/learn/no-fault-vs-at-fault-car-insurance-states/).
glossary.example: Sam is hurt when another driver runs a stop sign, but Sam was speeding. His damages total $50,000, and fault is split 60% to the other driver and 40% to Sam. In California (pure), Sam recovers 60%, which is $30,000. In Texas (51% bar), he also recovers $30,000, because 40% is below the bar. Now flip it: if Sam were 55% at fault, California would still pay him 45% ($22,500), while Texas, Georgia and Colorado would pay him nothing.
glossary.whyItMatters: A few percentage points can be the difference between a fair settlement and nothing, especially near the 50% and 51% bars. Insurers build fault percentages from police reports, photos, witnesses and your own words. Don't guess, apologise or speculate on a recorded call. Read [can I refuse a recorded statement to an insurance company](/qa/can-i-refuse-a-recorded-statement-to-insurance-company/), and consider [when to hire an insurance lawyer](/learn/when-to-hire-an-insurance-lawyer/) if the insurer's split seems unfair.

miniQuiz.question: You're 50% at fault for a crash in Georgia, with $40,000 in damages. How much can you recover from the other driver?

options.explanation: Correct. Georgia uses modified comparative negligence with a 50% bar, so at 50% or more you recover nothing from the other driver.
That's what you'd get in a pure comparative state like California or New York, not Georgia.
Your own share of fault always reduces or bars your recovery.

options.text: It depends on your PIP limit
options.explanation: Georgia doesn't require PIP. Comparative negligence decides recovery from the at-fault driver.

content.text: Comparative Negligence and Your Own Coverage

Fault splits affect what you recover from the other driver, not what your own first-party coverage pays. Your [PIP](/glossary/personal-injury-protection/) or MedPay, and your own collision coverage minus the deductible, pay regardless of fault. That's why fault-free coverage matters in at-fault states. See [PIP vs MedPay](/compare/pip-vs-medpay/).

Negligence rules are set by each state's statutes and courts and can change. This isn't legal advice. Source: [Bloomberg Law](https://pro.bloomberglaw.com/insights/litigation/contributory-and-comparative-negligence-by-state/).

scenarios.name: Alex
scenarios.situation: First-time homeowner with a partner and £350,000 mortgage. No children yet.
scenarios.coreQuestion: Do I actually need life insurance if I don't have children?
scenarios.scoutTake: Yes, because of joint mortgage liability! If something happened to Alex, their partner would suddenly face the entire monthly mortgage payment alone. To secure structural property risks, Alex also needs comprehensive building protection based on [replacement cost](/glossary/replacement-cost/) rather than purchase price—estimate rebuilding costs with our [Home Replacement-Cost Estimator](/home-replacement-cost-estimator/). Review our complete property primer in [Home Insurance Fundamentals](/learn/home-insurance-fundamentals/) and explore [Does Homeowners Insurance Cover Water Damage?](/qa/does-homeowners-insurance-cover-water-damage/).
keyRisks: Sole financial responsibility for the remaining £350,000 mortgage
Loss of joint household income to meet utility and living bills
Funeral and statutory administrative probate expenses
recommendedStrategy: Decreasing Term Life Insurance matched exactly to the 25-year repayment mortgage
Income Protection Cover replacing up to 60% of gross salary in case of long-term illness
Basic buildings and contents insurance as mandated by the mortgage lender
strategies: Purchase a joint decreasing term life policy or two single-life level term policies matching the mortgage debt—calculate needs on our [Term Insurance Calculator](/term-insurance-calculator/).

Attach an index-linked income protection policy covering 60% of gross pay to guard against long-term illness modeled in our [Disability Income Protection Calculator](/disability-insurance-calculator/).

Ensure buildings insurance covers full rebuild cost including site clearance and architect fees, and review [Actual Cash Value vs. Replacement Cost](/compare/actual-cash-value-vs-replacement-cost/) to prevent depreciation penalties.
Verify that standard water damage exclusions are endorsed back onto the policy as detailed in [What is an Exclusion in Insurance?](/learn/what-is-an-exclusion-in-insurance/).

scenarios.name: Jordan
scenarios.situation: Software designer financing a $28,000 vehicle. Has basic state liability auto insurance.
scenarios.coreQuestion: What does 'Full Coverage' actually mean, and what am I missing?
scenarios.scoutTake: California state minimum liability ($15k/$30k/$5k) only covers damage you cause to other people. It pays $0 to fix your own car if you crash or if it gets stolen. Upgrading to a full coverage package that balances [Comprehensive vs. Collision](/compare/comprehensive-vs-collision/) protects both your vehicle and your net worth. Evaluate your deductible threshold on our [Car Insurance Deductible Calculator](/car-insurance-deductible-calculator/) and review our legal analysis on [Can Insurance Drop You After a Claim?](/qa/can-insurance-drop-you-after-a-claim/).
keyRisks: If the car is totaled, state minimum liability pays $0 for repairs
If the car is financed, the auto lender contractually requires collision and comprehensive
State minimum liability limits ($15,000) are dangerously low in modern accidents
recommendedStrategy: Add Collision & Comprehensive coverage with a $500 or $1,000 deductible
Increase Bodily Injury Liability to at least $100,000 / $300,000
Add GAP insurance if loan balance exceeds the market value of the car
strategies: Raise bodily injury and property damage limits from statutory minimums to at least 100/300/100 using our [Car Insurance Coverage Calculator](/car-insurance-calculator/).

Add collision and comprehensive coverage with a $1,000 [deductible](/glossary/deductible/) to balance monthly cash flow against catastrophic vehicle loss as explained in [Deductible vs. Premium](/compare/deductible-vs-premium/).

Incorporate Uninsured/Underinsured Motorist Protection (UM/UIM) since 16%+ of California motorists operate without insurance—read [What Happens If You Crash Without Insurance?](/qa/what-happens-if-you-crash-without-insurance/).
Understand vehicle total loss payout rules based on [actual cash value](/glossary/actual-cash-value/) by reading our [Complete Car Insurance Guide](/learn/car-insurance-guide/).

scenarios.name: Sarah & David
scenarios.situation: Married couple with a 2-year-old toddler and a C$650,000 home mortgage.
scenarios.coreQuestion: How do we protect our child's university education and family home without overspending?
scenarios.scoutTake: Avoid expensive whole life policies pushed by commissioned agents. A 20-year level term policy gives Sarah and David C$1,000,000 in coverage each for pennies on the dollar compared to whole life. Model your household protection horizon with our [Term Insurance Calculator](/term-insurance-calculator/) and our [Insurance Needs Calculator](/insurance-needs-calculator/). Read our actuarial breakdown on [Term vs. Whole Life: Which is Better?](/compare/term-vs-whole-life/) and check [How Much Life Insurance Do I Need (Rule of Thumb)?](/qa/how-much-life-insurance-do-i-need-rule-of-thumb/).
keyRisks: Loss of one income would force home sale or deplete emergency savings
Future university tuition and childcare costs (approx C$18,000/year)
Disability impacting the primary income earner before retirement
recommendedStrategy: 20-Year Level Term Life Insurance: C$1M coverage on both parents
Critical Illness and Long-Term Disability supplemental benefits
Clear legal wills appointing guardians and naming contingent beneficiaries
strategies: Secure separate 20-year level term policies for both spouses rather than a joint-first-to-die policy to ensure independent protection for each parent.
Designate each other as primary [beneficiary](/glossary/beneficiary/) and establish a testamentary trust as contingent beneficiary for minor children.
Calculate total coverage to replace 10 years of household income plus the remaining mortgage balance using our [Life Insurance Calculator](/life-insurance-calculator/).
Confirm tax-free death benefit treatment under national tax laws as outlined in [Is Life Insurance Payout Taxable?](/qa/is-life-insurance-payout-taxable/).

scenarios.name: Marco
scenarios.situation: Freelance web developer renting an apartment in Berlin with no employer benefits.
scenarios.coreQuestion: What insurances are legally required vs. strongly recommended for EU freelancers?
scenarios.scoutTake: In Germany, health insurance is legally mandatory, and personal liability (Haftpflichtversicherung) is culturally and financially essential to prevent personal bankruptcy. As a freelancer, Marco's greatest single financial vulnerability is a long-term illness that stops billable hours. Learn how to protect your monthly baseline with our [Disability Income Protection Calculator](/disability-insurance-calculator/) and review our deep dive in [Long-Term vs. Short-Term Disability](/learn/long-term-vs-short-term-disability/).
keyRisks: Unlimited personal liability if an accident injures someone or damages property
Losing client income during extended illness without employer sick pay
State healthcare system penalties for lapsing coverage
recommendedStrategy: Statutory (GKV) or Private (PKV) Health Insurance tailored for Selbstständige
Private Liability Insurance (Privathaftpflicht) with at least €10M coverage limit (approx €5/mo)
Occupational Disability Insurance (Berufsunfähigkeitsversicherung) to safeguard earnings
strategies: Maintain statutory health insurance (GKV) or choose an expat-friendly private plan (PKV) while tracking your annual [out-of-pocket maximum](/glossary/out-of-pocket-maximum/) with our [Out-of-Pocket Cost Calculator](/health-insurance-calculator/).

Secure an independent Occupational Disability policy (Berufsunfähigkeitsversicherung) covering at least 70% of net monthly living expenses—see [Short-Term vs. Long-Term Disability: Do You Need Both?](/qa/short-term-vs-long-term-disability-do-you-need-both/).
Obtain a €5,000,000 to €10,000,000 private liability policy (Privathaftpflicht) to protect against third-party property damage and bodily injury claims.
Conduct an annual coverage checkup using our [8-Point Policy Review Checklist](/policy-review-checklist/) to eliminate uncovered exclusions defined in [Glossary: Exclusion](/glossary/exclusion/).

scenarios.name: Denise
scenarios.title: Denise's Insurance Decision
scenarios.situation: Retired teacher and longtime homeowner in a coastal Florida county. Her insurer of 12 years exited the state citing overall risk exposure, and a company she'd never heard of sent a renewal offer.
scenarios.coreQuestion: My homeowners insurer is leaving Florida and I got a renewal offer from a company I've never heard of — is this a scam, and should I accept it?
scenarios.scoutTake: An unfamiliar name on a Florida renewal notice usually means your old carrier transferred renewal rights, not that you're being scammed — but verify it yourself rather than assuming. See our full breakdown on [whether Slide Insurance is going out of business](/qa/is-slide-insurance-going-out-of-business/) and [compare Florida homeowners options](/compare/florida-homeowners-insurance/) before accepting or declining.
keyRisks: Accepting an unverified renewal offer without confirming licensing could leave a coverage gap if the offer is fraudulent
Letting the old policy lapse while shopping around leaves the home completely uninsured
Assuming 'unfamiliar' automatically means 'unstable' can lead to overpaying for a legacy brand when a newer, well-rated insurer is actually available
recommendedStrategy: Verify the new insurer's license status directly through the Florida Office of Insurance Regulation before accepting or declining
Check the company's AM Best or Demotech financial-strength rating rather than relying on brand recognition alone
Get at least one additional quote from a different licensed carrier before the old policy's expiration date
strategies: Confirm licensing on Florida's OIR company lookup before accepting a renewal from an unfamiliar carrier — see our full breakdown on [Slide Insurance's standing](/qa/is-slide-insurance-going-out-of-business/).
Compare admitted carriers, Citizens, and newer entrants side by side using our [Florida homeowners insurance comparison](/compare/florida-homeowners-insurance/).
Re-run your dwelling coverage numbers with our [Home Insurance Cost Calculator](/home-insurance-calculator/) whenever your premium changes significantly.

scenarios.name: Megan
scenarios.title: Megan's Insurance Decision
scenarios.situation: Marketing coordinator rear-ended in stopped traffic. Carries a standard full-coverage auto policy and needed to report a claim quickly to arrange a rental car and repair estimate.
scenarios.coreQuestion: I searched online for my insurer's claims number after an accident, called a third-party site's listing, and it was disconnected — how do I avoid losing time reporting a claim?
scenarios.scoutTake: Third-party 'contact number' aggregator sites are frequently outdated or scraped, not verified against the insurer's own current records — this cost Megan 45 minutes she didn't need to lose. Always go to your insurer's own site or your ID card first. See our breakdowns on [Dairyland's real contact channels](/qa/dairyland-insurance-phone-number/) and [Haven's contact number](/qa/haven-insurance-contact-number/), and run an [8-Point Policy Health Check](/policy-check/) before you ever need to make this call.
keyRisks: Delayed claim reporting can push back rental car authorization and repair scheduling by hours or days
Third-party 'contact number' aggregator sites are frequently outdated or scraped, not verified against the insurer's own records
Calling a sales/quotes line instead of claims adds transfer time during an already stressful event
recommendedStrategy: Save your insurer's verified claims number, from your ID card or official app, directly into your phone before you ever need it
File claims through your insurer's official app or online account whenever possible, bypassing the phone number problem entirely
Keep a written log of contact attempts, times, and reference numbers any time you're reporting an active claim
strategies: Verify your insurer's claims number directly through their official site or app rather than a search-result aggregator — cross-check using our guide on [Dairyland's real contact channels](/qa/dairyland-insurance-phone-number/).
Confirm your coverage limits are adequate before you ever need to call, using our [Car Insurance Coverage Calculator](/car-insurance-calculator/).
Run an [8-Point Policy Health Check](/policy-check/) annually so you already know your coverage and claims process before an accident happens.

scenarios.name: Alan
scenarios.title: Alan's Insurance Decision
scenarios.situation: Homeowner in a Los Angeles wildfire-risk zone. Placed coverage through a managing general agency with a surplus-lines (non-admitted) carrier partner after being dropped by his prior admitted insurer.
scenarios.coreQuestion: My neighbor and I both got insurance 'through the same company' but I just learned mine is non-admitted and his is admitted — what does that actually mean if my insurer ever fails?
scenarios.scoutTake: The MGA's brand name on your policy isn't the [underwriting](/learn/what-is-insurance-underwriting/) carrier — the admitted-vs-surplus-lines distinction only shows up when you check the actual carrier on your [declarations page](/learn/how-to-read-an-insurance-policy/). See our full answer on [whether Bamboo Insurance is admitted in California](/qa/is-bamboo-insurance-admitted-in-california/) and [compare wildfire-zone coverage options](/compare/california-wildfire-home-insurance/).
keyRisks: Non-admitted (surplus-lines) policies are not backed by California's guaranty fund (CIGA) if the carrier becomes insolvent
MGA brand names on marketing materials are not the actual underwriting carrier, which can obscure this distinction
Wildfire-zone surplus-lines placements can change between neighbors, or even between renewal cycles for the same policyholder
recommendedStrategy: Identify the actual underwriting carrier on your declarations page, not the MGA or agency brand name
Ask directly whether your specific policy is admitted or non-admitted before assuming based on a neighbor's coverage
Ask about newer admitted-capacity options at each renewal, since availability in wildfire zones has been expanding
strategies: Check whether your specific carrier is admitted or non-admitted using our full breakdown on [Bamboo Insurance's admitted status in California](/qa/is-bamboo-insurance-admitted-in-california/).
Compare admitted vs. surplus-lines wildfire coverage side by side with our [California wildfire insurance comparison](/compare/california-wildfire-home-insurance/).
Re-check your dwelling coverage adequacy using our [Home Insurance Cost Calculator](/home-insurance-calculator/) at every renewal.

scenarios.name: Kevin
scenarios.title: Kevin's Insurance Decision
scenarios.situation: IT consultant planning a weekend road trip from Texas into Mexico. Assumed his existing U.S. auto policy would cover him across the border.
scenarios.coreQuestion: I'm driving into Mexico this weekend — does my U.S. car insurance cover me, or do I need something else?
scenarios.scoutTake: A standard U.S. auto policy almost never satisfies Mexican law, even with a border-zone [rider](/learn/what-is-an-insurance-rider/) — and searching a generic name like '[Amigo insurance](/qa/is-amigo-insurance-legit/)' can send you to an unrelated company entirely. See [what Amigo Insurance actually refers to](/qa/what-is-amigo-insurance/) and [compare Mexico auto insurance options](/compare/mexico-auto-insurance/) before you cross the border.
keyRisks: A standard U.S. auto policy generally does not satisfy Mexican law, even with a border-zone rider
Mexican authorities can impound a vehicle after an accident without proof of Mexican-admitted liability coverage
Searching generic brand names like 'Amigo insurance' can return unrelated companies rather than an actual Mexico-insurance provider
recommendedStrategy: Buy a short-term Mexican tourist auto policy from a Mexican-admitted carrier before crossing the border
Confirm the policy explicitly names a Mexican-admitted underwriting carrier, not just a border-zone add-on
Purchase coverage online in advance rather than waiting to arrange it at the border crossing
strategies: Confirm whether you actually need a Mexico-specific insurer using our breakdown on [what 'Amigo Insurance' actually refers to](/qa/what-is-amigo-insurance/).
Compare a dedicated Mexico tourist policy against relying on your U.S. policy with our [Mexico auto insurance comparison](/compare/mexico-auto-insurance/).
Check your baseline U.S. liability limits with our [Car Insurance Coverage Calculator](/car-insurance-calculator/) before you travel.

scenarios.name: Emily
scenarios.title: Emily's Insurance Decision
scenarios.situation: First-time car buyer shopping for auto insurance online. Filled out what looked like a single quote form and received calls from several unrelated agents within the hour.
scenarios.coreQuestion: I filled out one online insurance quote form and now several different agents are calling me — did someone sell my information without my consent?
scenarios.scoutTake: [Lead-generation](/compare/verify-insurance-quote-site-before-entering-information/) quote forms are built to distribute one submission to several participating partners, not just one company — the consent for this is usually in [fine print](/learn/how-to-read-an-insurance-policy/) you agreed to when submitting. See [what QuoteLab actually is](/qa/what-is-quotelab/) and [how agencies use these platforms to get clients](/qa/how-to-get-clients-for-insurance-business/) for both sides of this.
keyRisks: Lead-generation quote forms typically distribute your information to multiple partner agents and carriers, not just one company
Consent for this kind of contact is usually buried in fine print you agree to when submitting the form
Comparison-site quotes can produce more follow-up calls than a single direct-insurer quote request
recommendedStrategy: Read the consent disclosure on any quote form before submitting your contact information
Search for a specific insurer's official site directly if you'd prefer only one company's quote
Ask unwanted callers to stop contacting you — reputable companies are required to honor that request
strategies: Understand what kind of company generated all the calls with our guide on [what QuoteLab actually is](/qa/what-is-quotelab/).
See the lead-generation side of this from an agency's perspective in [how to get clients for insurance business](/qa/how-to-get-clients-for-insurance-business/).
Compare the resulting quotes properly using our [Car Insurance Coverage Calculator](/car-insurance-calculator/) rather than picking based on whoever called first.

scenarios.name: Lauren
scenarios.title: Lauren's Insurance Decision
scenarios.situation: Marketing manager on an employer-sponsored PPO with a $2,500 deductible and $6,000 out-of-pocket maximum, recently diagnosed with a condition requiring an in-network specialist, monthly medication, and physical therapy.
scenarios.coreQuestion: Diagnosed mid-year with a condition needing specialist visits, ongoing medication, and physical therapy — how much will Lauren actually pay out of pocket, and in what order does her coverage kick in?
scenarios.scoutTake: Lauren's situation is a textbook illustration of how [deductible](/glossary/deductible/), coinsurance, and [out-of-pocket maximum](/glossary/out-of-pocket-maximum/) stack together in a single plan year. Because her diagnosis happened mid-year, all of her costs for the rest of the year count toward the same $2,500 deductible and $6,000 out-of-pocket max — meaning a bad month early on can make the rest of the year far cheaper than people expect. See [what does health insurance actually cover?](/learn/what-does-health-insurance-actually-cover/) for how these mechanics interact with specific benefit categories, and confirm whether her physical therapy visits are capped annually using [does health insurance cover chiropractic care?](/qa/does-health-insurance-cover-eye-exams-dermatologist-chiropractic/) as a reference point for how visit caps commonly work.
keyRisks: Physical therapy visit caps that could leave later sessions in the year fully out-of-pocket even after the deductible is met
A specialist referral requirement under her plan type that, if skipped, could result in a claim denial rather than just a higher copay
Prescription costs that may sit in a separate drug-specific deductible or tier structure rather than counting toward the same $2,500 medical deductible
recommendedStrategy: Confirm whether prescription costs apply to the same deductible or a separate pharmacy deductible before assuming all costs stack together
Get the required referral from her primary care physician before the first specialist visit to avoid a coverage denial

Track running totals toward both the deductible and out-of-pocket maximum using the plan's online member portal, since hitting the $6,000 out-of-pocket max means 100% coverage for the rest of the plan year
scenarios.estimatedMonthlyCost: $180 - $420 / month until the $6,000 out-of-pocket maximum is reached, then $0 in cost-sharing for the remainder of the plan year
strategies: Request an itemized breakdown from the insurer showing exactly how much of the deductible and out-of-pocket maximum has been met so far, using our [Out-of-Pocket Cost Calculator](/health-insurance-calculator/) to project the rest of the year.

Ask the physical therapy provider directly how many visits per year are covered under Lauren's specific plan before scheduling an extended treatment course, referencing the visit-cap pattern in [does health insurance cover chiropractic care?](/qa/does-health-insurance-cover-eye-exams-dermatologist-chiropractic/).

If Lauren later considers a job change, check whether COBRA or a new employer's plan would reset her deductible and out-of-pocket progress — see [COBRA continuation coverage](/glossary/cobra-continuation-coverage/) for how that transition works.

scenarios.name: Marcus
scenarios.title: Marcus's Insurance Decision
scenarios.situation: Owner of a 14-employee logistics company currently offering no group health plan, losing candidates to competitors that offer benefits, and comparing structural options for the first time.
scenarios.coreQuestion: With 14 employees and no benefits history, should Marcus set up a standard fully-insured small-group plan, join a PEO, or consider level-funding — and what does each actually cost and risk?
scenarios.scoutTake: At 14 employees, Marcus sits right at the edge of what most level-funded carriers will underwrite, which narrows his realistic choice mostly to a standard fully-insured small-group plan or a PEO health plan. See [level-funded vs. fully-insured health insurance](/compare/level-funded-vs-fully-insured-health-insurance/) for why group size matters so much here, and [PEO health plan](/glossary/peo-health-plan/) for how the co-employment pooling structure could get Marcus large-employer-style pricing despite his small headcount. Either path is far better for recruiting than his current no-benefits position, given how much [does health insurance cover pregnancy and maternity care?](/qa/does-health-insurance-cover-pregnancy-maternity-care/) and similar core-benefit questions come up in candidate conversations.
keyRisks: Setting up a standard small-group plan without shopping multiple carriers, potentially overpaying for comparable coverage
Underestimating the loss of direct HR control that comes with a PEO's co-employment structure
Choosing based on premium alone without comparing network quality and the specific benefit exclusions (like GLP-1 weight-loss drug coverage) each option applies
recommendedStrategy: Get quotes for a standard fully-insured small-group plan from at least three carriers before comparing further

Request a detailed PEO proposal showing exactly which benefits, network, and pricing employees would get under the pooled structure, using [PEO health plan](/glossary/peo-health-plan/) as a framework for the right questions to ask

Compare both proposals against the [ACA marketplace vs. employer-sponsored coverage](/compare/aca-marketplace-vs-employer-sponsored-health-insurance/) baseline to sanity-check whether employer-sponsored coverage of either type is actually the better deal for his specific employee group
scenarios.estimatedMonthlyCost: $450 - $650 per employee per month for a standard small-group plan; often 10-20% lower per employee under a well-negotiated PEO arrangement, depending on the PEO's overall risk pool
strategies: Shop at least three fully-insured small-group carrier quotes before deciding, using our [Out-of-Pocket Cost Calculator](/health-insurance-calculator/) to compare real employee cost-sharing, not just the headline premium.

Ask any PEO candidate directly how co-employment would affect Marcus's existing HR processes and who becomes the employer of record, referencing [PEO health plan](/glossary/peo-health-plan/) for the specific trade-offs to probe.

If Marcus's business ever separates from a PEO later, plan ahead for the transition using [COBRA continuation coverage](/glossary/cobra-continuation-coverage/) as a reference point for how continuation options work when an employer-sponsored plan changes.

scenarios.name: Maria
scenarios.title: Maria's Insurance Decision
scenarios.situation: First-time boat buyer, just purchased a financed 24-foot center console for weekend fishing and beach trips, docked at a local marina.
scenarios.coreQuestion: Is boat insurance actually required in Florida, and what should I realistically budget for it?
scenarios.scoutTake: Florida doesn't legally mandate boat insurance — see our full [Boat Insurance by State](/learn/boat-insurance-by-state-requirements-costs/) guide — but Maria's boat is financed and dockside at a marina, and both her lender and the marina will require proof of coverage regardless of state law. Because she's in a hurricane-exposed state, she also needs to understand [named storm deductibles and hurricane plan requirements](/learn/boat-insurance-and-hurricane-season/) before her first June-through-November season. Her [liability limit](/learn/what-is-a-coverage-limit/) deserves real thought too, not just the bare minimum — see [How Much Boat Liability Insurance Do You Actually Need?](/qa/how-much-boat-liability-insurance-do-you-need/).
keyRisks: A serious on-water collision or passenger injury exceeding a low liability limit
Hurricane or named storm damage while the boat is docked, without a hurricane plan on file
An uninsured boater causing an accident, since Florida doesn't require other boaters to carry coverage either
The lender's loan agreement requiring specific physical damage coverage Maria hasn't yet confirmed she has
recommendedStrategy: Full coverage boat insurance (not liability-only), since the boat is financed and the lender will require physical damage protection — see [Liability-Only vs. Full Coverage Boat Insurance](/compare/liability-only-vs-full-coverage-boat-insurance/)
A liability limit meaningfully above Florida's non-existent state minimum, sized to her actual assets
Uninsured boater coverage, given how common uninsured boating is in a state with no mandate — see [Uninsured Boater Coverage](/qa/uninsured-boater-coverage/)
A written hurricane plan on file with her insurer before her first storm season, including her marina's haul-out procedure
strategies: Confirm her lender's specific physical damage and liability requirements in writing before finalizing coverage.
Set liability limits closer to $300,000-$500,000 rather than any bare minimum, given her personal asset exposure — model this with our [Insurance Needs Calculator](/insurance-needs-calculator/).
Add uninsured boater coverage given how many recreational boaters in Florida carry no insurance at all.

Review her policy's named storm deductible and haul-out reimbursement benefit before hurricane season begins, and confirm her marina's own hurricane procedure separately in [Marina Insurance](/learn/marina-insurance/).

scenarios.name: Tom
scenarios.title: Tom's Insurance Decision
scenarios.situation: Recently retired, selling his house and moving full-time onto a 42-foot houseboat permanently moored at a marina slip.
scenarios.coreQuestion: If I'm going to live on this houseboat full-time, does my old homeowner's insurance transfer over, or do I need something completely different?
scenarios.scoutTake: A standard homeowner's policy doesn't extend to a floating structure — Tom needs a dedicated [Houseboat Insurance](/learn/houseboat-insurance/) policy that blends marine coverage with the personal property and liability protection his old home policy used to provide. Because he's moving aboard full-time rather than using it occasionally, he needs to disclose that liveaboard status accurately, since it changes how much personal property and personal liability coverage he actually needs. He should also understand what his marina's own policy does and doesn't cover for him as a slip tenant — see [Marina Insurance](/learn/marina-insurance/) — and, since his houseboat is permanently moored rather than cruising, confirm with his insurer whether it's underwritten more like a floating home or a conventional vessel.
keyRisks: Personal belongings and everyday liability (a guest injured aboard, for example) not being covered if he assumes marine liability alone is enough
Understating full-time liveaboard status to save on premium, which can jeopardize a future claim
Assuming the marina's own insurance covers his personal property or the houseboat itself, when it typically only covers the marina's own dock and premises
Fire, storm, or sinking risk without confirming exactly what perils his specific stationary-houseboat policy actually covers
recommendedStrategy: A dedicated houseboat policy disclosing full-time liveaboard use, including personal property and personal liability coverage comparable to what a homeowner's policy would have provided
Confirmation from his insurer on whether the permanently moored structure is underwritten as a floating home or a conventional vessel, since this affects which perils are actually covered
His own contents and liability coverage, independent of whatever his marina's policy covers for its own property
A clear understanding of any usage or navigation restrictions tied to his specific liveaboard policy
strategies: Get houseboat-specific quotes rather than assuming a marine policy or homeowner's policy alone will work — see [Houseboat Insurance](/learn/houseboat-insurance/) for what to ask.
Disclose full-time liveaboard status accurately, even if it means a higher premium than understating it would.
Confirm personal liability coverage extends to everyday incidents aboard, not just boating-specific accidents.
Ask his marina directly what its own policy covers for slip tenants, and don't assume it extends to his personal belongings or the houseboat itself — see [Marina Insurance](/learn/marina-insurance/).

scenarios.name: Elena
scenarios.title: Elena's Insurance Decision
scenarios.situation: Elena's 14-year-old son needs a full course of orthodontic treatment to correct a significant overbite. She has an employer-sponsored dental PPO with an orthodontic rider covering 50% coinsurance up to a $1,500 lifetime maximum per covered person. Her son's San Diego orthodontist quoted $6,800 for traditional metal braces — near the higher end of California pricing, which runs above the national average due to regional labor and lab costs.
scenarios.coreQuestion: My insurance covers half the cost of braces — so why do I still owe almost $6,000 out of pocket?
scenarios.scoutTake: Elena's plan isn't underperforming — this is exactly how orthodontic riders are designed to work. The 50% coinsurance applies, but only up to the $1,500 lifetime maximum, meaning insurance contributes a flat $1,500 regardless of the total treatment cost, not 50% of the full $6,800 bill. See the [complete dental cost comparison](/learn/dental-procedure-costs-with-and-without-insurance/) for how this lifetime-maximum structure differs from the annual maximums that apply to fillings and crowns. Because California orthodontic pricing runs above the national average, the gap between the quoted price and the fixed lifetime maximum is wider here than it would be in a lower-cost state for the identical treatment plan. Before assuming a second plan would help, it's worth running the [coordination of benefits math](/qa/can-you-have-two-dental-insurance-plans/) — a second plan's own separate lifetime maximum could meaningfully close this specific gap if her spouse has dental coverage through a different employer.
keyRisks: The $1,500 lifetime maximum is a flat dollar cap, not a percentage of the total bill, so a higher California quote widens the out-of-pocket gap compared to the national average price for the same treatment.
The lifetime maximum applies per person, per lifetime — not annually — so it can't be "saved up" or reset if a second child in the family also needs orthodontic treatment on the same plan.
Financing the remaining ~$5,300 through a third-party medical credit line rather than the orthodontist's own in-house plan could add interest charges if not paid off within a promotional period.
